titre: RBNZ’s Breman says chances of a December rate hike are high after surprise hold at 2.75%
titre_fr: RBNZ’s Breman says chances of a December rate hike are high after surprise hold at 2.75%
contenu:
Breman’s comments push back against the dovish reading ofWednesday’s holdand look aimed at steadying the New Zealand dollar, which she has said could add to imported inflation if it stays weak. Pricing of around 77% leaves room for further repricing toward a December hike if incoming data cooperates, which would support the currency and front-end yields. Her emphasis that timing is uncertain keeps the risk of a second hold alive, so the kiwi’s recovery may be gradual rather than sharp. Fuel prices remain the main external swing factor, linking the RBNZ path to oil and the Iran conflict.

-

A day after a hold that sank the kiwi, Breman is all but promising December, though she isn’t quite ready to put it in writing.

Summary:

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman said on Thursday that the chances of an interest rate hike in December are high, sharpening her guidance a day after the central bank surprised markets by leaving the official cash rate unchanged at 2.75%.

In an interview with the New Zealand Herald, Breman said every member of the monetary policy committee agrees that further increases in the cash rate are likely, though the timing remains uncertain and will depend on the economic outlook and how inflation develops. Asked directly about the odds of a move in December, she said they were high.

The comments go further than the signal the RBNZ gave on Wednesday, when it held rates but said additional hikes were likely. That decision caught markets off guard. Before the announcement, pricing had pointed to a hike as close to a certainty, and the New Zealand dollar fell sharply after the bank held. Markets now price around a 77% chance of a hike in December.

The hold was itself a close call, with the committee split 4-3 and Breman among the majority who argued that two recent rate increases warranted time to assess their effects. At her press conference after the decision, she said tightening could need to extend into restrictive territory and flagged concern that a weaker currency could add to imported inflation at a time when fuel costs have risen further.

Fresh data has added weight to that concern. A business survey released on Thursday showed the share of New Zealand firms planning to raise prices climbed to its highest since May, with cost expectations remaining very high.

Breman also sought to reassure the public, saying that despite an uncertain environment, the RBNZ would remain calm and focused on its mandate of returning inflation to target.

The December decision will come alongside the Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts and a new projected path for the cash rate. Until then, inflation indicators, labour market data and the currency will be key in determining whether the high chance of a hike becomes a reality.

titre: The view from China: CITIC Securities still sees a 25bp Fed hike in December
titre_fr: The view from China: CITIC Securities still sees a 25bp Fed hike in December
contenu:
CITIC’s call reinforces the market’s December hike pricing, but its view that the terminal rate stays near current levels points to a shallow end to the cycle rather than an extended run of increases. That combination supports the dollar into December, with less upside for Treasury yields further out. On oil, the brokerage sees no clear de-escalation path yet between the US and Iran, which argues for crude holding its risk premium. That in turn keeps upward pressure on the inflation backdrop the Fed is reacting to. Its note that dollar liquidity needs a fresh catalyst suggests funding conditions are unlikely to ease on their own in the near term.

---

Earlier:

---

From China, CITIC Securities sees one more Fed hike and then a plateau, with oil, not the Fed, setting the pace for what comes after.

Summary:

Chinese brokerage CITIC Securities still expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December, but sees the peak for this tightening cycle staying close to current levels, offering a view from China that broadly aligns with US market expectations.

In its assessment of the Fed’s October meeting, CITIC said the decision to hold, which left the policy rate at 3.75% to 4%, was in line with expectations. It noted that the post-meeting statement sounded more positive on growth, while guidance on the path for policy was more guarded. According to the brokerage, remarks from Fed officials after the meeting were softer in tone than in September. They pointed to tighter credit conditions and inflation expectations moving in the right direction, and flagged changes to the policy meeting schedule over the next two years.

That schedule change, announced by Chair Warsh, will see the Fed vote on rates at seven of its eight meetings next year and six in 2028, with the remaining sessions devoted to strategy.

Despite the milder tone, CITIC sees a December hike as its base case. Its view that the terminal rate is unlikely to move much above current levels implies the brokerage sees limited room for tightening beyond that move. The meeting itself showed hawkish pressure on the committee, with two officials dissenting in favour of an immediate hike.

The brokerage also linked the Fed outlook to the Middle East. It said recent developments are not yet enough to put the US and Iran on a clear and lasting path toward de-escalation, and that oil prices could remain high until the situation becomes clearer. That matters for the Fed because elevated energy costs feed directly into the inflation picture policymakers are trying to bring under control.

CITIC added that any further improvement in US dollar liquidity would require a new catalyst. For markets, the brokerage’s message is that the December decision and the course of US-Iran diplomacy remain the two key variables shaping both rates and oil into year end.

titre: NZ business confidence rises to +53 as pricing intentions hit highest since May
titre_fr: NZ business confidence rises to +53 as pricing intentions hit highest since May
contenu:
Firmer pricing intentions and inflation expectations stuck around 3.3% give the RBNZ little reason to ease off its tightening. The resilient activity readings also undercut any argument that the oil shock is crushing demand. For the New Zealand dollar, that is a modest support, though the currency’s weakness is itself feeding the services export boom. The oil link remains the main swing factor: ANZ’s data shows business sentiment tracking crude closely this year, so any renewed spike in prices tied to the Iran conflict would be the biggest threat to this resilience.

---

New Zealand business has taken the latest oil shock on the chin far better than it took the last one, but rising price plans mean theRBNZ will be watchingjust as closely as the bosses.

Summary:

New Zealand business confidence edged up in October and firms’ plans to raise prices climbed to their highest since May, the ANZ Business Outlook survey showed, suggesting the economy is weathering the renewed jump in oil prices better than many had feared.

Headline business confidence rose 1 point to +53, while expected own activity, which ANZ regards as the more reliable guide to the economy’s direction, eased 2 points to a still-solid +46. Reported past activity, which compares current trading with a year earlier, improved 4 points to +15, with every sector in positive territory.

Price pressures were mixed but leaned higher. A net 52% of firms expect to raise prices over the next three months, up 4 points, and the average expected price increase rose to 1.9%, the highest since June. Cost expectations held at a very high net 82%, while one-year-ahead inflation expectations were steady at 3.3%. ANZ noted that cost expectations have stayed contained despite higher fuel prices, but cautioned that firms are estimating increases from an already inflated starting point.

Among the other details, services firms’ export intentions jumped to their highest in 25 years, which ANZ linked to the weak New Zealand dollar, with tourism operators reporting strong forward bookings. Investment intentions slipped to +18 from +23, and employment intentions held at around +17. Wage expectations of around 2.8% suggest only marginal upside risk to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s wage forecasts, according to ANZ. Wellington recorded the highest regional confidence, while Canterbury was the lowest.

ANZ said the renewed rise in oil prices is a headwind for both New Zealand and the global economy, but that the survey matches what it is hearing from business owners: the confidence shock that brought activity close to a standstill in the second quarter has not been repeated. Some firms have been surprised by how well demand has held up despite price increases, while others are realising that continually putting off decisions such as investment carries its own risks.

With interest rates rising and pricing intentions firming, the next survey, due on November 30, will show whether that resilience can withstand both higher energy costs and tighter monetary policy.

titre: Hong Kong holds base rate at 4.25%: why the HKMA always moves in lockstep with the Fed
titre_fr: Hong Kong holds base rate at 4.25%: why the HKMA always moves in lockstep with the Fed
contenu:
For Hong Kong, the decision confirms that local borrowing costs stay tied to the Fed’s hiking path, regardless of domestic conditions. Mortgage holders and property developers are most exposed, because a December Fed hike would flow through to the base rate and from there to bank lending rates. The peg also means Hong Kong dollar assets carry US rate risk. Traders should watch Fed expectations, not the HKMA, when positioning for Hong Kong rate moves.

---

Earlier:

---

Hong Kong’s rate decisions are made in Washington, and with a December Fed hike widely expected, the city’s borrowers are along for the ride.

Summary:

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority kept its base rate unchanged at 4.25% on Thursday, as expected, following the US Federal Reserve’s decision to hold its policy rate at 3.75% to 4%. The outcome was never in doubt, and understanding why explains how Hong Kong runs monetary policy.

Hong Kong has operated its Linked Exchange Rate System since 1983. Under it, the Hong Kong dollar is held within a narrow band of HK$7.75 to HK$7.85 against the US dollar. The HKMA commits to buy or sell Hong Kong dollars at either edge of that range, which keeps the currency anchored to the greenback.

A fixed exchange rate comes with a trade-off: a city cannot run an independent interest rate policy while keeping its currency pegged. If Hong Kong rates drifted far from US rates, capital would flow toward whichever currency paid more, putting pressure on the peg. So Hong Kong effectively imports US monetary policy.

That link is written directly into the base rate formula. The rate is set at the higher of two measures: 50 basis points above the lower end of the Fed funds target range, or an average of short-term Hong Kong interbank rates, known as HIBOR. With the Fed’s range starting at 3.75%, adding 50 basis points produces exactly 4.25%. When the Fed moves, the HKMA follows.

Market forces back up the formula. If the Hong Kong dollar weakens to HK$7.85, the HKMA buys local currency, draining cash from the banking system and pushing interbank rates higher until the currency recovers. At the strong end, it sells Hong Kong dollars, adding liquidity and pushing rates down.

The practical consequence is that Hong Kong’s borrowing costs are set by conditions in the United States rather than at home. That matters now. The Fed held this week but signalled that inflation remains its priority, and markets widely expect a hike in December. If that happens, Hong Kong’s base rate is likely to rise in step, whatever the state of its own economy.

titre: Recap: Fed holds at 3.75%-4% in 10-2 vote as Cook dissents for a hike, December move in focus
titre_fr: Recap: Fed holds at 3.75%-4% in 10-2 vote as Cook dissents for a hike, December move in focus
contenu:
A hold with two hawkish dissents and no pushback from Warsh on December pricing keeps the bias firmly toward tightening, which supports Treasury yields and the dollar into year end. Cook’s dissent matters for rate expectations because it widens hawkish support beyond the committee’s usual hard-liners, strengthening the case that a December hike has broad backing. The dissent may also be read politically, given Trump’s efforts to remove her, which adds to scrutiny of Fed independence. Fewer scheduled rate decisions from next year mean each meeting carries more weight, and that could amplify market moves around those dates.

---

Earlier:

---

The Fed paused, but with two votes for a hike and a chair insisting the job isn’t done, the pause looks more like a breather than a turn.

Summary:

The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 on Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate at a range of 3.75% to 4%, pausing after last month’s increase, while leaving markets firmly expecting another hike in December, theWall Street Journalreported.

The decision itself was widely anticipated. The surprise lay in the dissents. Fed Governor Lisa Cook voted against the hold in favour of a higher rate, breaking with a record of consistently voting with the committee’s consensus since she joined the central bank more than four years ago. Cook, whom President Donald Trump has been trying to remove from her post for more than a year, had recently expressed concern that inflation remains a problem, but had not indicated she saw an urgent need for a further increase.

The second dissent, from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, was more in line with expectations. Hammack has been among the committee’s most hawkish members this year and also dissented in favour of tighter policy in April and July.

At his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Warsh sought to make clear that pausing did not mean the Fed was easing off its effort to bring inflation down. He said returning inflation fully to the 2% target was the overriding priority, that the Fed had recommitted to that goal since he took over, and that last month’s hike marked the start of action. Warsh acknowledged the Fed had not yet achieved price stability but said it was working toward it, and he offered little to challenge the market view that a December increase is coming.

Warsh also announced a change to the Fed’s meeting schedule. Next year, policymakers will vote on rates at only seven of their eight meetings, using the remaining session for a broader strategy discussion. In 2028, that will drop to six rate decisions, with two meetings set aside for strategy. The shift overhauls a calendar that has been in place for 45 years. Warsh first raised the idea internally over the summer.

The move fits his preference for a lower-profile Fed. The post-meeting statement has become shorter under his leadership, and he has opted out of the quarterly dot plot of officials’ projections.

With two officials already pushing for a hike, the December meeting now looms as the next key test of the Fed’s tightening path.

titre: The full statement from the October 2026 FOMC rate decision
titre_fr: The full statement from the October 2026 FOMC rate decision
contenu:
The full statement from the October 2026 rate decision:

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:

The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriateto ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

titre: The full statement from the Bank of Canada rate decision for October 2026. Hikes by 25 basis points
titre_fr: The full statement from the Bank of Canada rate decision for October 2026. Hikes by 25 basis points
contenu:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Media Relations

Ottawa, Ontario

October 28, 2026

Share this page on Facebook

Share this page on X

Share this page on LinkedIn

Share this page by email

The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%.

Since the JulyMonetary Policy Report, global economic activity has remained resilient, despite higher energy prices. In the United States, the economy continues to grow at a robust pace, supported by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area has been resilient and broad-based. After slowing in the second quarter, Chinese growth rebounded in the third quarter, owing to strength in exports and a pickup in fiscal spending. With persistently elevated oil prices and refinery margins, inflation has risen in most countries.

Given the ongoing resilience of the global economy, the Bank has revised up global GDP growth slightly to 3.1% in 2026, while growth in 2027 and 2028 remains unchanged from the July projection at 3.2%.

Global financial conditions have tightened since July. Advanced economy sovereign bond yields are higher. Equity and credit markets have been volatile due to uncertainty about the outlook for the AI sector. The Canadian dollar had weakened somewhat on US-dollar strength but has since recovered to around 71 cents – the same as assumed in the July Report.

Growth picked up in Canada through the middle of the year. GDP growth was 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to growth of about 2% in the third quarter. This is stronger than expected in the July Report. Consumer spending has been solid, even with slow population growth. Business investment rebounded, reflecting oil and gas sector activity and spending on machinery and equipment. Despite ongoing weakness in sectors affected by US tariffs, exports overall have strengthened, owing to robust US demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the changing trade environment. The unemployment rate has been around 6½% for several months. A broad set of indicators continue to point to some excess supply in the economy.

Owing to new US tariffs, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter of 2026, before picking up again in 2027. This rebound is supported by business investment, exports and fiscal measures. Consumption growth is expected to moderate and housing to remain relatively weak.

The Canadian economy is expected to grow 1% in 2026, and 2% in 2027 and 2028. This is a somewhat stronger overall growth projection than the July Report. This forecast is still subject to considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding Canada-US trade relations.

Given persistently high oil prices, CPI inflation has been around 3% since April and is expected to rise to about 3½% by the end of the year. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2% in September and measures of core inflation remain close to 2%. But cost pressures are building, with high fuel prices raising the costs of production and transportation. Imported industrial and electronics input prices have also increased. While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, Bank surveys suggest cost pass-through will increase over the next year. Near-term household and business inflation expectations have risen, while longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices and increased pass-through adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection. CPI inflation is expected to average 3% in 2027, a percentage point above the July projection, then come down to 2% in the middle of 2028. The main sources of uncertainty around this forecast are developments in the Middle East and businesses’ responses to cost pressures.

In the outlook, inflation is higher and more persistent than in the July Report. Growth has picked up this year and is expected to recover further. Against this backdrop, Governing Council decided to increase the policy rate to reduce the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services. There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability.

-------------------------------------------------------------

titre: RBNZ’s Breman: more hikes likely at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory
titre_fr: RBNZ’s Breman: more hikes likely at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory
contenu:
Breman’s guidance partly reverses thedovish read of the hold. Signalling likely hikes at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory, should push December pricing back up, support front-end yields and help the New Zealand dollar recover some of its losses. Her explicit worry about a weak currency feeding imported inflation acts as a soft floor for the kiwi, since further falls make a hike more likely. Oil is the main swing factor: fuel is already lifting inflation toward 4.4%, so higher crude, especially if a US strike on Iran escalates after the midterms, would make a December hike much more likely. The guidance also narrows the policygap with the RBA, which may capAUD/NZDafter this morning’s divergence.

---

The RBNZ held, then Breman spent the press conference telling markets not to read too much into it: more hikes are likely, and they may go further than planned.

Summary:

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman said further interest rate increases are likely at coming meetings and could take policy into restrictive territory, sounding a more hawkish note at her media conference hours after the central bank surprised markets by holding its official cash rate at 2.75%.

Breman said the Monetary Policy Committee agreed that tighter policy is likely to be required, conditional on how the economy evolves. She said it is likely the RBNZ will deliver further rate increases at upcoming meetings, and that additional tightening might be needed even into restrictive territory, meaning rates high enough to actively slow the economy rather than simply removing stimulus. She also said the committee discussed whether rates could need to rise further than its existing projected path for the OCR.

The currency featured prominently. Breman said the committee discussed the decline in the New Zealand dollar and is concerned that, if the currency remains weak, it could add to imported inflation. The RBNZ’s statement noted that the trade-weighted exchange rate has fallen around 3% since early September, at a time when fuel prices have risen further because of disruptions in global energy markets.

Breman explained the decision to hold rather than hike in terms of the economic outlook, while acknowledging the committee did look at market pricing, which had priced roughly a 90% chance of a hike. She said conditions for returning inflation to target remain favourable, pointing to wage growth running below levels consistent with inflation at the 2% midpoint. That echoed the majority view in the committee’s 4-3 vote, which argued the two recent hikes give it time to assess their effects.

The governor also said the committee discussed the risk of a correction in AI-related market assets, building on the RBNZ’s warning that financial stability risks have increased because of high debt and opaque financing arrangements for some AI investment.

Looking ahead, Breman said partial inflation indicators and labour market data in the coming weeks will be important for the committee’s assessment. The next decision is due with the December Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts and a new projected path for the OCR.

The press conference left markets with a mixed message: a decision that leaned dovish, and guidance from the governor that leaned hawkish. With a minority already pushing for a hike and Breman now signalling increases are likely, December is shaping up as a live meeting, particularly if fuel prices stay high and the currency remains weak.

titre: RBA’s Bullock: Inflation is far too high
titre_fr: RBA’s Bullock: Inflation is far too high
contenu:
By saying it is hard to completely look through supply shocks, Bullock signalled that the RBA is less willing to ignore the energy-driven jump in prices than theRBNZ was earlier. Any further rise in crude therefore adds directly to the case for an RBA hike. Her blunt language (morehere earlier), together withfirmer core inflationand her view that demand still exceeds supply, supports pricing for a move on November 2 and 3, and backs the Australian dollar and front-end yields. The contrast with the RBNZ’s hold sharpens the policy divergence, whichfavours AUD/NZD. Bullock’s refusal to give guidance leaves some uncertainty, but the overall tone tilts clearly hawkish.

---Bullock didn’t pre-announce a hike, but “far too high” and “difficult to look through supply shocks” are about as close as a central banker gets without saying it.

Summary:

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is far too high, as she and her senior colleagues responded to hotter-than-expected September quarter CPI data during a Senate committee hearing on Wednesday, days before the RBA Board meets to decide on interest rates.

Bullock said the latest figures were consistent with the upside risks to inflation the RBA had flagged, and that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks such as the current surge in energy prices. She added that domestic demand is still running ahead of the economy’s capacity to supply it, a sign that price pressures are not only being imported. She declined, however, to give guidance on the Board’s decision on November 2 and 3.

Her deputy, Andrew Hauser, said the CPI numbers were in line with expectations but still too high, while Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said inflation came in stronger than the RBA had expected in August. The two comments are consistent: the data broadly matched what economists forecast ahead of the release, but ran above the path in the RBA’s August Statement on Monetary Policy. Hunter also said she does not expect Australia to fall into recession.

The remarks followed a data release that added to the RBA’s concerns. The trimmed mean, the central bank’s main gauge of underlying inflation, rose 1.0% in the September quarter and 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected, while monthly headline inflation climbed to 4.3% in September. Earlier in the hearing, before the data was released, Bullock had said inflation was likely to run higher than the RBA’s August forecasts, citing re-escalating conflict in the Middle East, much higher energy prices and a labour market that looks a little tighter than the RBA had judged.

Bullock’s comment on supply shocks is significant. Central banks often look through one-off jumps in prices such as fuel, on the basis that they fade on their own. By saying that is hard to do completely, Bullock signalled that the RBA is concerned about higher energy costs spreading into broader prices and into inflation expectations, particularly with underlying inflation already above target.

The RBA has raised its cash rate by a cumulative 100 basis points this year. Bullock has said a key question for next week’s meeting is whether that tightening will be enough to return inflation to the 2% to 3% target in a reasonable time. While she stopped short of signalling a move, the combination of firmer core inflation, a tight labour market and the Governor’s blunt language keeps another hike firmly in play. The Board’s decision next week will be accompanied by updated forecasts.

titre: RBNZ holds OCR at 2.75% in surprise 4-3 vote, says tighter policy still likely
titre_fr: RBNZ holds OCR at 2.75% in surprise 4-3 vote, says tighter policy still likely
contenu:
Oil sits at the centre of the call: the RBNZ expects fuel to lift inflation to 4.4% in the December quarter, but the majority chose to look through the direct effects for now, betting that weak demand will limit pass-through. With a hike close to fully priced, the hold is likely to hit the New Zealand dollar and pull front-end yields lower. The 4-3 split and the guidance that tighter policy is still likely should limit how far December pricing unwinds. Policy divergence is now sharp.Hotter Australian core inflation this morningand ahawkish Bullockcontrast with a cautious RBNZ, which points to upside for AUD/NZD into the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3. The RBNZ’s warning about opaque AI financing and an abrupt global downturn adds a dovish tail risk that markets had largely ignored.

---

Background:

---

The RBNZ blinked: with a hike almost fully priced, four of seven members chose to wait, betting that weak demand will contain the fuel shock, while keeping December firmly in play.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand unexpectedly held its official cash rate at 2.75% on Wednesday, with the Monetary Policy Committee split 4-3, wrong-footing markets and every major local bank that had forecast a third consecutive hike. The committee said tighter policy is still likely to be needed, but that the timing remains conditional on the economic outlook.

Governor Anna Breman, Carl Hansen, Rebecca Williams and Prasanna Gai voted to hold, while Hayley Gourley, Paul Conway and Karen Silk voted for a 25 basis point increase to 3%. Markets had priced roughly a 90% chance of a hike ahead of the decision, and ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Westpac and Kiwibank had all expected a move.

The majority argued that the two hikes delivered in July and September give the committee time to assess their effects. Annual CPI inflation eased to 3.7% in the September quarter from 4.1% in June, lower than the RBNZ had expected, as the indirect effects of higher fuel prices proved smaller than assumed. These members noted that wage growth remains subdued, medium-term inflation expectations are stable and there is little evidence so far that businesses are using higher costs to widen their margins. They also stressed the risk of a weak recovery in household spending and investment.

The minority took a more hawkish view. They argued that core inflation has been above levels consistent with the target midpoint for some time, raising the risk that inflation becomes entrenched in price setting as the Middle East conflict and higher freight and shipping costs persist. With aggregate growth proving resilient, they said acting now would guard against sustained price pressure and could reduce the need for larger rate increases later, favouring a move to around the midpoint of the neutral range.

Fuel remains central to the outlook. The RBNZ said fuel prices have risen further because of ongoing disruption in global energy markets, including lost refining capacity and shipping problems, while the New Zealand dollar’s trade-weighted index has fallen around 3% since early September. It expects annual inflation to rise to 4.4% in the December quarter, largely on the basis of current oil futures prices, but cautioned that near-term forecasts are highly uncertain given volatility in oil and refined fuel prices. Excluding vehicle fuels, annual inflation rose to 3.0%, and core measures have climbed to around the top of the 1% to 3% target band. Price increases have also broadened, with 56% of the CPI basket, by weight, rising by more than 3% over the year.

The domestic economy is recovering unevenly. Export-exposed regions are benefiting from high commodity prices, strong goods demand and rising tourist numbers, while household consumption remains weak, employment growth is subdued and house prices continue to fall. The household saving rate is estimated at 3.7%, well above its 10-year average of 1%, suggesting consumers remain cautious.

The committee also flagged growing global risks. It said financial stability risks have increased since September, citing high debt levels and opaque, complex financing arrangements for some AI investments, and warned that rising long-term interest rates could expose vulnerabilities and that a global downturn could occur abruptly. Two members, Gai and Breman, said that risk should be factored into judgements about the neutral rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, rather than relying on midpoint estimates.

The RBNZ made clear its next move could go either way. Members said information over the next six weeks could change the appropriate stance in either direction. Further tightening could be warranted if domestic price pressures fail to ease or broaden beyond what costs and normal pass-through can explain, while subdued pressures could justify holding. A sharp global downturn could even lead to easing.

The next decision comes with the December Monetary Policy Statement, which will include updated forecasts. Breman holds a media conference at 3pm New Zealand time, which is 02:00 GMT.

titre: BlackRock sees one more Fed hike this year, calls market pricing for more too hawkish
titre_fr: BlackRock sees one more Fed hike this year, calls market pricing for more too hawkish
contenu:
BlackRock’s view supports the front end of the Treasury curve. If the Fed sounds less aggressive than markets fear this week, two-year yields have the most room to fall, which would steepen the curve. Its caution on the long end, where it still sees yields rising as competition for capital intensifies, matches the heavy-supply theme flagged this week by Fitch and S&P. Neutral positioning on US equities, with a continued tilt to AI and tech, suggests BlackRock expects volatility around policy, not a broad selloff. A dovish-leaning Fed would also cap the dollar. Higher oil remains the main risk to the “less hawkish than priced” view, since further energy-driven inflation would test it.

---

Earlier:

---

BlackRock thinks the Fed will hike once more and then stop, and it is positioning for that by owning short-dated Treasuries while staying wary of long bonds.

Summary:

BlackRock expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates once more by the end of the year but sees market pricing for further tightening as overly hawkish, a view that underpins its preference for short-dated US Treasuries over longer bonds, according to the BlackRock Investment Institute’s weekly commentary.

The Fed’s policy decision this week, its second-to-last meeting of 2026, takes centre stage after a hotter-than-expected September CPI report that showed price pressures broadening. Even so, BlackRock said it does not view the recent tightening as the start of a new, sustained hiking cycle. It noted that markets have partly scaled back expectations for further hikes since the Fed’s September meeting, moving closer to its own view, though it still regards the remaining pricing as excessive.

That stance shapes BlackRock’s fixed income positioning. The asset manager is overweight short-dated US Treasuries, saying much of the repricing it had anticipated has already taken place and that expectations for further Fed hikes look too high. It favours the front end of the curve for attractive income and a greater breakeven buffer, meaning yields are high enough to absorb some further rise in rates before investors start losing money.

BlackRock is neutral on long-dated Treasuries. It said higher yields offer attractive income and a bigger cushion against further rate increases, but it still sees room for long-term yields to rise as competition for capital intensifies, a pressure that comes as governments and companies, including those investing in AI infrastructure, borrow heavily.

On equities, BlackRock is neutral on US stocks overall. It said strong AI fundamentals remain supportive, but policy uncertainty could fuel volatility in the near term. Within the market, it continues to favour AI and technology.

Taken together, BlackRock’s positioning amounts to a bet that the Fed will tighten less than markets expect, while acknowledging that the long end of the curve remains vulnerable to supply pressure and that equity gains may depend increasingly on the AI theme. The Fed’s statement and any guidance on the pace of further hikes will be the first test of that view.

titre: MUFG sees RBNZ hiking to 3% today but under-delivering on pricing, flags NZD downside
titre_fr: MUFG sees RBNZ hiking to 3% today but under-delivering on pricing, flags NZD downside
contenu:
MUFG’s call puts the risk squarely on the New Zealand dollar: with a hike almost fully priced, the currency’s G10 outperformance this month depends on the RBNZ endorsing a much steeper path than MUFG expects. Neutral or “wait and see” language could trigger a repricing of the roughly three and a half further hikes priced, pulling front-end yields lower and weighing on the kiwi, with AUD/NZD a likely beneficiary ahead of the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3. A hawkish surprise would delay that repricing, not prevent it, in MUFG’s view. Oil remains the main counterweight: further gains in crude would push up New Zealand’s fuel-driven inflation and make the market’s more aggressive path harder to unwind.

---

Earlier:

---

MUFG thinks the RBNZ will hike today and then disappoint, arguing that New Zealand’s spare capacity cannot justify the rate path markets have priced, which leaves the kiwi’s recent strength on borrowed time.

Summary:

MUFG expects the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise its official cash rate by 25 basis points today but to fall short of the hawkish path markets have priced, leaving the New Zealand dollar exposed to downside risk, according to a preview from the bank.

The decision is due at 01:00 GMT on Wednesday, which is 21:00 US Eastern on Tuesday. MUFG said the rates market is almost fully priced for a 25 basis point hike, which would take the OCR to 3% and mark a third consecutive increase. The bank expects the RBNZ to deliver that move, but sees only one further hike after today, to a peak of 3.25%. By MUFG’s reckoning, market pricing implies around three and a half additional hikes beyond today’s decision, with three hikes in total priced by March.

The gap matters for the currency. MUFG noted that the New Zealand dollar has been the third-best performing G10 currency this month, a run it said depends on the RBNZ delivering a hawkish hike and guidance strong enough to validate current pricing. Without that, the support from rate expectations could fade.

MUFG’s case for a shallower path rests on the domestic economy. It said third-quarter inflation came in slightly weaker than expected, which it believes reflects the degree of spare capacity, or unused resources, in the New Zealand economy. The bank also pointed to the jump in the unemployment rate to 5.6% in the second quarter, the highest since the third quarter of 2015. In MUFG’s view, that slack means the economy will not require as much tightening as markets are pricing.

The bank said the risks for the New Zealand dollar are skewed to the downside. Even if the RBNZ delivers a hawkish hike today, MUFG expects investors to question at some point how many increases are priced, and it forecasts the currency to underperform over its forecast horizon.

MUFG’s view puts it at the dovish end of expectations. Locally, ANZ has pencilled in a pause in December, while ASB and Westpac expect the OCR to reach 3.5% by February. With today’s meeting a Monetary Policy Review without updated forecasts or a rate track, the tone of the RBNZ’s statement is likely to decide which of those paths markets lean toward.

titre: All 5 major NZ banks expect RBNZ to hike to 3% today, but split on how far rates will go
titre_fr: All 5 major NZ banks expect RBNZ to hike to 3% today, but split on how far rates will go
contenu:
A 25bp hike is close to fully priced, so the New Zealand dollar is likely to trade on guidance, not the move itself. Language that leaves the door open to more tightening would back the hawkish paths from ASB and Westpac and lift front-end yields. “Wait and see” wording, as Kiwibank expects, would favour ANZ’s pause view and could pull back some of the pricing for a peak. A split vote would add volatility either way. Oil is the swing factor beyond today: further gains in crude would add to New Zealand’s fuel-driven inflation and strengthen the case for 3.5% or higher. AUD/NZD traders face back-to-back central bank risk, with the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3.

---

Earlier:

Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Breman

---

New Zealand’s banks are united on a hike to 3% today, but their paths after that range from an ANZ pause to a Westpac peak of 4%, so the RBNZ’s guidance matters more than the move.

Summary:

All five of New Zealand’s major banks expect the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 3% today, which would be its third consecutive hike, but they are divided on how much further the central bank will need to go.

The decision is due at 14:00 New Zealand time, which is 01:00 GMT on Wednesday and 21:00 US Eastern on Tuesday. Markets have roughly 90% of a hike priced in, according to ASB, and BNZ said a decision to hold would come as a material shock.

The consensus has firmed over the past week. Before the September quarter CPI release, Westpac was the outlier calling for a pause, but it now expects a hike today. Kiwibank, which said in September the economy looked too weak for further tightening, also expects a move, though it sees the RBNZ pairing the hike with “wait and see” language before holding.

The banks’ rate paths diverge after today. ANZ has lightly pencilled in a pause in December, with chief economist Sharon Zollner describing 3% as a more comfortable level for the RBNZ to sit at. ASB expects further hikes in December and February, taking the OCR to a peak of 3.5%, and has lifted its estimate of the neutral rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, to around 3.5%. BNZ said the RBNZ should signal that more tightening is coming. Westpac has the most hawkish track, with hikes in December and February to 3.5%, followed by further increases in June and September 2027 to a peak of 4%. Westpac also said a split committee vote was very possible.

The drivers are oil and the currency. Higher fuel prices and a weaker New Zealand dollar have lifted the inflation outlook, and while annual inflation eased to 3.7% in the September quarter, banks expect it to climb back toward 4.5% to 4.7% by the December quarter.

Today’s meeting is a Monetary Policy Review rather than a full Monetary Policy Statement, so it will not include updated forecasts or a projected rate track. That leaves the tone of the short statement, any hint at the next move and the voting record as the main signals for markets. The decision also lands 10 days before New Zealand’s November 7 general election, although Governor Anna Breman has said the election is not a factor in policy decisions.

---

titre: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign
titre_fr: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign
contenu:
Fitch’s December call fits the view that the Fed is still on a hiking path, which supports front-end Treasury yields and the US dollar and argues against any near-term easing. The more telling signal for credit is the split it describes: investment-grade spreads near multi-year lows while CCC yields have blown out. Heavy hyperscaler issuance on top of Treasury supply raises the risk that new deals need bigger concessions even where credit quality holds up. For equities, putting a recession scenario next to AI capex keeps the spotlight on any sign that hyperscalers are scaling back spending plans.

---

I spotted the headlines from Fitch overngiht and just bringing it to investingLive now. Fitch trails behind S&P and Moody's but I doubt their analysis and conclusions would be too much different.

----

Fitch still calls US credit benign overall, but its December Fed hike call, record private credit defaults and an AI-driven recession scenario show the pressure building on the weakest borrowers.

Summary:

Fitch Ratings expects the US credit outlook to remain broadly benign, even as higher-for-longer interest rates and rising AI-related funding needs put interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers under pressure, according to a Fitch Wire commentary published Tuesday alongside its fourth-quarter US credit brief.

The ratings agency has lifted its US growth forecasts for both 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 percentage point to 2.1%, pointing to resilient consumer spending and AI-driven private investment. Fixed investment is forecast to grow 4.8% this year and 4.6% next year. On policy, Fitch expects the Federal Reserve to raise its policy rate to 4.25% in December and keep it there through 2027, which it says will sustain pressure on borrowers who need to refinance at higher costs.

Funding conditions are also being shaped by heavy Treasury supply and increased borrowing by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators, to pay for AI capital spending. Fitch said US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months of 2026, while corporate bond issuance climbed around 25%. The picture across the credit spectrum is uneven. Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while yields on CCC-rated debt, the lowest rung of high yield, have widened by about 480 basis points since the start of the year.

Fitch described AI investment as both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. IT-related private investment grew around 18% year on year in the second quarter, but the agency warned that intensifying competition and cheaper open-weight models could weaken the pricing power of AI service providers and prompt a rethink of hyperscaler capex plans over the next one to three years. Under Fitch’s adverse AI equity-correction scenario, the US would fall into recession, with GDP contracting 0.6% in 2027. Its sector-level AI stress test found broad resilience, with material risks concentrated in services, data centres, and telecommunications, media and technology.

Higher rates are weighing most heavily on housing-related sectors and lower-rated borrowers. Fitch’s US private credit default rate reached a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and the agency expects leveraged loan defaults to rise toward the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end forecast range.

The commentary leaves the Fed’s December decision and the durability of AI spending as the two variables most likely to determine whether a benign outlook for credit overall holds up for its weakest borrowers.

Fitch Ratings expects the US credit outlook to remain broadly benign, even as higher-for-longer interest rates and rising AI-related funding needs put interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers under pressure, according to a Fitch Wire commentary published Tuesday alongside its fourth-quarter US credit brief.

The ratings agency has lifted its US growth forecasts for both 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 percentage point to 2.1%, pointing to resilient consumer spending and AI-driven private investment. Fixed investment is forecast to grow 4.8% this year and 4.6% next year. On policy, Fitch expects the Federal Reserve to raise its policy rate to 4.25% in December and keep it there through 2027, which it says will sustain pressure on borrowers who need to refinance at higher costs.

Funding conditions are also being shaped by heavy Treasury supply and increased borrowing by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators, to pay for AI capital spending. Fitch said US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months of 2026, while corporate bond issuance climbed around 25%. The picture across the credit spectrum is uneven. Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while yields on CCC-rated debt, the lowest rung of high yield, have widened by about 480 basis points since the start of the year.

Fitch described AI investment as both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. IT-related private investment grew around 18% year on year in the second quarter, but the agency warned that intensifying competition and cheaper open-weight models could weaken the pricing power of AI service providers and prompt a rethink of hyperscaler capex plans over the next one to three years. Under Fitch’s adverse AI equity-correction scenario, the US would fall into recession, with GDP contracting 0.6% in 2027. Its sector-level AI stress test found broad resilience, with material risks concentrated in services, data centres, and telecommunications, media and technology.

Higher rates are weighing most heavily on housing-related sectors and lower-rated borrowers. Fitch’s US private credit default rate reached a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and the agency expects leveraged loan defaults to rise toward the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end forecast range.

The commentary leaves the Fed’s December decision and the durability of AI spending as the two variables most likely to determine whether a benign outlook for credit overall holds up for its weakest borrowers.

titre: Japan services PPI picks up to 3.7% as August revised lower, backing BoJ hike path
titre_fr: Japan services PPI picks up to 3.7% as August revised lower, backing BoJ hike path
contenu:
The downward revision to August makes the September print more hawkish than the headline suggests: services prices are accelerating, not just holding. That adds weight to the case for the BoJ’s Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, and supports December hike pricing, lending the yen modest support into Friday. Short-end JGB yields could edge higher as markets price a firmer BoJ tone. Oil-driven cost pressure from the Iran conflict remains a background inflation risk, but this data shows domestic, labour-driven pressure building too. The vote split and Ueda’s press conference remain the bigger yen catalysts.

---

Earlier:

---A quiet downward revision to August turned Japan’s in-line services print into an acceleration, and that’s the version of the story the BoJ will be reading this week.

Summary:

Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% year on year in September, in line with expectations and faster than a downwardly revised 3.5% gain in August, Bank of Japan data showed on Tuesday. The pick-up points to mounting service-sector price pressure ahead of a BoJ meeting this week that is expected to leave rates on hold while signalling further tightening ahead.

The revision changes the picture. August’s reading was initially reported at 3.7%, which had suggested September would merely match the prior month. With August now at 3.5%, the September figure marks an acceleration rather than a steady pace, a more hawkish read for policymakers watching whether inflation is becoming entrenched in the domestic economy.

The index tracks the prices companies charge each other for services such as transport, communications, finance, real estate, advertising and equipment leasing. The BoJ watches it closely for evidence of how far firms are passing rising labour costs on to service prices, a central part of its case that wage growth and inflation are reinforcing each other. A faster pace suggests that pass-through is gathering momentum rather than fading.

The data contrast with the goods side, where producer price inflation slowed to 6.8% in September from 7.6% in August as fuel subsidies eased some raw-material costs. Services prices rising while goods inflation slows suggests domestic, labour-driven pressure is taking over from imported costs as the main driver.

The BoJ concludes a two-day meeting on Friday and is expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25%, after raising it in September, while signalling it is ready to continue lifting borrowing costs as price pressures build. Most economists expect the next hike in December. The key focus is whether the bank’s updated Outlook Report effectively declares that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, a step it has never taken since adopting the goal in 2013.

Today’s acceleration strengthens the case for that declaration and makes it harder for the board members who opposed September’s hike to argue for easier policy.

titre: Moody’s Zandi says a Fed hike this week would be a mistake as 5% yields do the tightening
titre_fr: Moody’s Zandi says a Fed hike this week would be a mistake as 5% yields do the tightening
contenu:
Zandi’s view runs against market pricing for at least one more hike this year, so it’s more a marker for the doves than a market mover. It does sharpen focus on the tension in this week’s Fed decision. Oil is the pivot: crude climbing back toward wartime peaks on Iran tensions lifts inflation and keeps the Fed on its hiking path, while also squeezing real incomes in a way that strengthens Zandi’s growth warning. With 10-year yields near 5% and credit spreads wider, any hawkish surprise from the Fed risks further pressure on rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and leveraged borrowers. A skip with hawkish guidance, as Goldman Sachs expects, would keep December live.

---

Earlier:

---

Zandi’s case is simple: the bond market has already tightened for the Fed, and hiking into an oil shock risks doing the economy’s real damage for it.

Summary:

Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has warned that raising interest rates at this week’s Federal Reserve meeting would be a mistake, arguing that the bond market is already doing the tightening for the central bank and that a policy error now ranks among the growing risks facing the US economy.

Writing on X on Monday, Zandi pointed to the sharp rise in borrowing costs since the Fed’s September hike. The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering around 5%, fixed mortgage rates are above 7% and corporate bond spreads have widened. In his view, that rise in market rates is already restraining the economy, which leaves no need for the Fed to add to it. The FOMC meets on October 27 and 28, with the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00% after September’s quarter-point increase, and markets pricing at least one more hike before year-end.

Oil sits at the centre of his argument. With prices climbing back toward their wartime peaks on tensions with Iran, Zandi said higher energy costs will push up inflation, but warned that rate hikes cannot fix a supply problem. Instead, he argued, higher oil prices will erode real wages and consumer spending, and tightening into that squeeze risks tipping the economy into trouble.

Zandi also pointed to Moody’s risk matrix, which ranks threats to the economy over the next 12 to 18 months by likelihood and potential damage. He said it contains a lot of red, with risks including an AI stock sell-off, a Fed misstep, intensifying wars, trade escalation and financial repression.

The warning is consistent with his earlier stance. Zandi described September’s hike as a serious mistake and warned in late September that higher rates were already damaging the economy. The Fed’s case for tightening rests on inflation that remains well above target, with headline PCE estimated at 3.8% in August and core at 3.4%, alongside price pressure from oil, tariffs and AI investment.

Some on Wall Street expect the Fed to wait this week. Goldman Sachs sees a skip in October followed by a hike in December, which would leave Zandi’s argument as much a test for the December meeting as for this one.

titre: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac’s Ellis says read the data calls
titre_fr: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac’s Ellis says read the data calls
contenu:
For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials’ data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff’s downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read.

---

Yesterday:

---

The RBA has never been chattier, but Westpac’s Luci Ellis says traders hunting for promises should listen instead to how it reads the data, because that is where the real signal lives.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of Australia is talking more often, in more places and on more technical subjects than it did a few years ago, but it still is not promising anything about the path of interest rates, according to Westpac Group chief economist Luci Ellis. In a note on RBA communication, she argues that the clearest signal of future policy lies in how officials interpret incoming data, rather than in any form of forward guidance.

Ellis counts 58 public engagements on the RBA’s speeches page so far this year, already matching the total for all of last year and above the 52 recorded in 2024. Delivery has shifted too, away from set-piece policy speeches toward semi-scripted fireside chats and interviews across a wide range of media, part of a broader effort to explain decisions to the general public at a time when rates are rising but households are not the main source of inflation.

That wider reach can confuse markets, Ellis says, because different audiences call for different tones. The post-meeting press conference is aimed at the public, so a Governor who sounds softer there may simply be acknowledging that policy is causing pain, much as a doctor warns that a treatment might hurt without stopping it. Where tone differs, she argues, pre-drafted material such as the minutes is a more reliable guide to the Board’s thinking than off-the-cuff answers.

The content has also become more technical. Officials increasingly discuss estimates of unobservable variables such as neutral interest rates and financial conditions, and a spot check of readability scores suggests recent speeches are harder to read than those from 2021. The RBA has also stressed that monetary policy works through several channels beyond mortgage repayments, though Ellis notes that if the cashflow channel is the smallest, as the Deputy Governor suggested, a small group of households is bearing a heavy cost for limited effect on inflation.

The practical takeaway is to read the RBA’s interpretation of data. Ellis highlights that the Governor described the labour market as a little tight after the September meeting, even though the Board’s statement did not, and says the Deputy Governor’s recent hawkish tone was no surprise given staff’s downbeat view of supply capacity. With Senate Estimates coinciding with the quarterly CPI release ahead of the November decision, there will be plenty for markets to parse.

Ellis when she was with the Reserve Bank of Australia.
contenu_fr:
For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials’ data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff’s downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read.

titre: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
titre_fr: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
contenu:
A hold with an effective 2% declaration and a firm Ueda press conference would support the yen and pull December hike pricing forward, pushing short-end JGB yields higher. The asymmetric risk is the vote: if the two reflationist members switch from opposing a hike to calling for a cut, the dovish signal could outweigh the hawkish language and trigger yen selling. USD/JPY is also exposed to this week’s Fed meeting. A surprise US hike that sent the pair sharply higher is the kind of emergency that, per the Nikkei report, could put a back-to-back BoJ move on the table. Oil-driven inflation pressure from the Iran conflict adds to the case for a firmer BoJ tone.

---

Still to come:

---

The BoJ is set to stand still on rates this week while moving a big step forward on rhetoric, unless two dovish dissenters steal the headlines and the yen pays for it.

Summary:

The Bank of Japan’s policy meeting on October 29 and 30 is unlikely to deliver a rate hike, but it could mark a turning point in how the central bank describes inflation, according to a preview from MUFG. The bank expects the BoJ’s updated Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached the 2% price stability target, which would take the normalisation pursued under Governor Kazuo Ueda into a new phase.

A back-to-back increase looks off the table. MUFG noted a Nikkei report citing a senior BoJ official as saying the bank would consider consecutive hikes only in a serious emergency. MUFG said that could in theory include a sharp rise in USD/JPY following an unexpected rate hike by the Federal Reserve, though it sees that scenario as unlikely. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September.

Ueda has already been laying the groundwork for a firmer message. Speaking after last week’s G20 meeting, he said underlying inflation was now broadly close to 2% and that the BoJ could not tolerate a further rise. That built on his remarks after the September meeting that the policy phase had changed, and reinforced the bank’s sharper focus on containing inflation. MUFG therefore expects the tone of Ueda’s post-meeting press conference to be relatively hawkish.

External pressure points in the same direction. US Treasury Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne was reported over the weekend as saying Japan is no longer in a deflationary environment and that its monetary policy should adjust accordingly.

The main risk MUFG flags comes from inside the board. The two members who voted against the September rate hike could dissent again, this time opposing a hold and instead calling for a rate cut. MUFG said such a move by the BoJ’s reflationist members would reinforce the bank’s dovish image and would likely prompt yen selling, undercutting the hawkish signal from the Outlook Report and Ueda’s press conference.

For markets, the week’s outcome may therefore hinge less on the rate decision than on the vote split and the language around underlying inflation.

titre: NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite
titre_fr: NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite
contenu:
The Shadow Board result adds to the case for a hike at the October review, although several members still favour a pause, so a hold would not be a shock. A hike paired with a clear signal of a prolonged pause could limit any boost to the New Zealand dollar, while a hold with hawkish guidance would keep year-end hike pricing alive. Oil is the swing factor: members tied much of the inflation risk to fuel prices and the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would strengthen the case for more tightening. The next inflation release is the near-term catalyst for NZ rate pricing.

---

Earlier:

---

Oil and a sliding kiwi have tipped most of NZIER’s Shadow Board toward another RBNZ hike, though the minority wants the central bank to let its earlier tightening do the work.

Summary:

A majority of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research’s Monetary Policy Shadow Board has recommended that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points at its upcoming October Monetary Policy Review, which would take the rate to 3% from 2.75%. The group, which is independent of the central bank, said renewed pressure on global energy prices and a recent fall in the New Zealand dollar have increased the upside risks to inflation enough to justify another increase now.

The board was not unanimous. Several members argued that the RBNZ should give the increases already delivered more time to work through an economy that remains soft, with a cyclically weak labour market. One bank chief economist said there is a case to slow the pace of tightening, noting that while the short-term inflation picture looks more threatening, the medium-term outlook has not shifted, and that business and consumer surveys show no sign yet of second-round price effects.

Those favouring a hike pointed to a combination of pressures. Members cited the rebound in oil prices, a weaker currency, stronger-than-expected growth and core inflation that has stayed elevated, with one arguing that looking through these shocks has not returned inflation sustainably to the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target band. Another member framed the decision as finely balanced, warning that with the conflict in Iran continuing, fuel-driven price pressures may prove less temporary than hoped.

A further view urged the bank to deliver the move and then signal a prolonged pause, arguing that clarity on the end of the tightening cycle would do more for business confidence than leaving the threat of further increases hanging over the economy.

Looking further out, most members agreed the OCR should rise over the coming year, with views of where it should sit in twelve months ranging between 3% and 4%. Some said the pace of further tightening should depend on how underlying inflation, inflation expectations and the recovery evolve. Several members flagged upcoming inflation data as important, and that release is likely to shape whether the RBNZ moves now or waits until year-end, as many commentators expect.

---

The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) is an independent economic research and consulting organisation based in Wellington, and its Monetary Policy Shadow Board is a panel of economists, academics and business leaders that meets ahead of each Reserve Bank of New Zealand decision. The key distinction is that the board says what the RBNZ should do, not what it will do. Each member assigns percentage weights to the policy options they prefer, and NZIER averages those preferences into a collective view. That makes the result a policy recommendation rather than a forecast or preview of the likely outcome. The two can differ: this month most members favour a hike, even though, as one member noted, many commentators expect the RBNZ to pause until year-end. NZIER says the exercise is also meant to encourage informed debate, show how a board structure might work, and explore how members could use probabilities to express uncertainty. The board is independent of the RBNZ, and members’ views are their own, not those of their employers.

titre: Major central banks take centre stage this week but will there be any surprises?
titre_fr: Major central banks take centre stage this week but will there be any surprises?
contenu:
The central bank bonanza is back in town this week, with five big names lining up to announce their latest monetary policy decisions. After all the recent drama involving oil prices, bond yields, and the stock market, perhaps it is time for central bankers to have their say again.

Of note, we will have the RBNZ, BOC, Fed, ECB, and BOJ all on the agenda this week. And looking to market pricing, traders seem to have a pretty good idea of what to expect already from the decisions to come. So, the only question is will there be any surprises? Let's see.

TheRBNZwill kick things off on Wednesday with traders fully pricing in a 25 bps rate hike. That leaves little suspense surrounding the decision itself, although traders will be watching for clues on whether policymakers are prepared to tighten further in December.

Then, theBOCwill follow later in the day with markets pricing in roughly 83% odds of a 25 bps rate hike. The pricing reflects relatively strong conviction with just a bit of room for a potential surprise. But all else being equal, the central bank should deliver as expected this week. Perhaps the bigger question is whether another rate hike will be needed as policymakers continue to wrestle with inflation risks. So, that will be the key risk trigger for the loonie reaction in the aftermath.

After that, we will have theFedto finish off the day with traders assigning around 91% odds of no change in interest rates. As such, the decision itself won't be the main talking point here. Instead, it will all rest on Fed chair Warsh's pess conference. His remarks will be closely scrutinised, especially with rising oil prices complicating the inflation outlook while recent weakness in the stock market raises fresh concerns about growth.

And on Thursday, it is then on theECBto take the wheel with markets pricing in roughly 90% odds of a hold. But with energy-driven inflation pressures building and European growth showing signs of weakness, ECB president Lagarde will have a lot to address with her press conference. In particular, traders will be looking for clues on December, where expectations for another rate hike have been building.

Finally, theBOJwill round things off on Friday with traders seeing roughly 98% odds of no change in interest rates. But with the yen still struggling and underlying inflation holding near 2%, the focus will be on whether policymakers offer any stronger signals about a potential move in December. BOJ governor Ueda's press conference is likely to steer clear of any pre-commitment though, so there might not be much to the key risk event here; all else being equal.

All things considered, I wouldn't expect the interest rate decisions alone to deliver much drama this week. As we've seen time and again, it is often what central bankers say about their next move that ends up stirring markets the most. So, that is what I'll be watching more closely with the meeting decisions and press conferences this week.

titre: BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
titre_fr: BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
contenu:
With a hold widely expected, yen and JGB moves are likely to hinge on the vote and Ueda’s guidance. Hawkish dissent from Takata or Tamura, or language pointing to the next meeting, would probably bring December pricing forward and offer the yen some support. A unanimous hold paired with cautious messaging could see hike expectations drift toward January, keeping the yen soft. Front-end JGB yields remain the most sensitive gauge of shifts in timing, and Friday’s Tokyo CPI print lands on the same day as the decision, adding to the potential for volatility.

---

Earlier:

---

Ueda is in no rush to hike again this week, but he has made clear the BOJ is not done, with the debate now about whether the next move comes in December or January.

Summary:

The Bank of Japan is expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at its October 29-30 meeting, with Governor Kazuo Ueda signalling there is no need for back-to-back increases but that rates will have to rise further toward a neutral level, according to Mace News.

The board raised the rate from 1% in a 7-2 vote in September. Since then, Ueda has said that oversized or consecutive hikes are typically reserved for situations where inflation is rising rapidly beyond target, and that the bank is making pre-emptive adjustments to avoid being forced into abrupt tightening later. Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and its main goal is to stabilise inflation around that level. Board member Junko Koeda also argued last week that the bank should not become overly cautious about raising rates.

Mace News sees the most likely path as a hike to 1.50% in December or January, followed by a rise to 1.75% in March or April. That would continue a faster pattern of tightening every three to four months.

The board is broadly divided into four camps. Hawks Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura may start pushing for the next increase on Friday, setting the stage for possible action at the December 17-18 meeting. At the dovish end, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato have dissented against recent hikes.

On the data front, Tokyo’s October CPI is forecast to show inflation at 2.7% to 2.8% across all three key measures, partly reflecting the fading impact of local fiscal support. September jobs, industrial production and retail sales figures are also due.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda

titre: ECB set to hold at 2.50% as Morgan Stanley sees December as natural moment for next hike
titre_fr: ECB set to hold at 2.50% as Morgan Stanley sees December as natural moment for next hike
contenu:
With a hold almost fully priced, the euro’s reaction will turn on whether Lagarde validates December hike expectations or keeps full optionality, and a noncommittal message could see some tightening priced out and weigh on the single currency. The Fed decision a day earlier sets the backdrop for EUR/USD, so a hawkish Fed followed by a cautious ECB would be the most euro-negative combination. Higher oil linked to the Middle East conflict remains the main upside risk to eurozone inflation and to hike pricing. French government bonds are exposed to any sign that the ECB sees the recent rise in yields as a concern rather than welcome tightening, and Friday’s flash inflation and GDP data could quickly reprice December either way.

---

Earlier:

---

The ECB looks set to take a breather this week, letting higher bond yields do some of its work, while December shapes up as the meeting where the next hike gets decided.

Summary:

The European Central Bank is widely expected to keep its deposit rate unchanged at 2.50% on Thursday, pausing after September’s rate increase as policymakers weigh an uncertain economic outlook against inflation that is still running well above target.

Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note that there is so far no sign of significant indirect or second-round effects from the latest energy shock on inflation, and that the recent rise in long-term bond yields is already providing a degree of additional tightening. Together, those factors remove any urgency to deliver another hike this week, the bank said, adding that December, when policymakers will have fresh data and updated staff projections, looks like the more natural moment to shift the policy stance.

That view is widely shared. In a Reuters poll conducted earlier this month, 70 of 73 economists expected the ECB to hold in October, while 64 of 73 saw a further 25 basis point increase in December, a sharp reversal from the previous survey, when most thought the tightening cycle was over.

The jump in sovereign bond yields, particularly in France amid concerns over its debt and budget, is likely to be on policymakers’ minds. ING economists argue that the French fiscal crisis and higher yields are already tightening financial conditions, making a hold very likely and pushing any further decision to December. Commerzbank expects the deposit rate to rise to 2.75% in December and then stay there throughout 2027, pointing to an anticipated decline in oil prices and the dampening effect of higher yields as reasons against further moves.

Investors will focus on President Christine Lagarde’s press conference for any signals on the prospect of further rate increases in the coming months. The decision is due at 13:15 GMT (09:15 ET), with the press conference following at 13:45 GMT (09:45 ET).

The data calendar is busy. Germany’s Ifo business survey for October is out on Monday, the GfK consumer confidence survey follows on Wednesday, and eurozone business and consumer surveys are due on Thursday. On Friday, provisional third-quarter eurozone GDP figures will be released alongside flash October inflation data from individual countries, including France and Germany, offering an early read on whether the case for a December hike is strengthening.
