titre: Fed's Beige Book:  Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
titre_fr: Fed's Beige Book:  Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
contenu:
The October Beige Book shows an economy losing a step while inflation pressures intensify. The national summary dropped its headline characterization of activity entirely. August said activity “increased modestly”; this report simply tallies the districts and notes that reports outside of manufacturing “indicate little growth overall.” Philadelphia and New York both slowed to slight growth from modest, while Chicago slipped to flat. Manufacturing is doing the heavy lifting, led by a sharp pickup in Dallas along with continued strength in data centers, power generation and defense.

The consumer has stalled. August described spending as growing slightly; now most districts report little or no change, and more than half said spending was being driven by high-income households. The strain is spreading up the income ladder. San Francisco said pressure on lower-income families has spread to middle-income households, and New York noted rising 401(k) hardship withdrawals and earned-wage advances. In Cleveland, a record 87% of surveyed nonprofits said their clients’ finances deteriorated. Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco all flagged a drop in Canadian tourists.

Prices are the biggest shift. In August, only one district reported robust price growth and only one said the pace had accelerated. Now it’s three and four, respectively. Higher oil prices showed up in every district report, with diesel the most commonly cited cost. The forward-looking language is more concerning for the Fed: firms expect further increases as hedges and fixed contracts expire and get repriced. Philadelphia’s future prices indexes are among the highest readings in 35 years, and a New York food manufacturer said it hadn’t seen such broad-based pressures since the pandemic. Consumer-facing firms still can’t pass costs through, so margins are getting squeezed.

Hiring was marginally better than August, but real wages are a growing issue. Boston staffing contacts said raises are lagging inflation, and cost-of-living demands came up in several districts. AI also featured more prominently, with five districts reporting firms trimming staff through attrition, delaying hiring or planning fewer new jobs.

Higher rates are a new theme. Rising mortgage rates slowed housing further in Philadelphia, Kansas City said CRE loan spreads rose substantially, and Dallas bankers turned pessimistic, citing the Mideast conflict, inflation and the increase in the fed funds rate.

The FOMC meets Oct. 27-28 and along withtoday's CPI report, this adds to the case for hiking rates. We will hear from Chair Warsh late tomorrow.

titre: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
titre_fr: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
contenu:
The stakes around the October Federal Reserve meeting suddenly got much higher.

Today's US CPI report was hot across the board, including in core measures that are less volatile than the energy-driven headline. The bond market quickly repriced on the data, with US 2-year yields now up 15 basis points on the day to 4.94%.

In the Fed funds futures market, pricing is now right at 50/50 for a hike or hold this month. It's also critical to note that the Fed goes into the blackout period on Saturday.

That leaves just three days to shape the narrative if the Fed doesn't want to go into the meeting with raised stakes. That starts today with a 1:30 pm ET speech from Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin. I'm a fan of Barkin's level-headed style and he usually represents the core views of the Fed, so that's one to watch especially closely. That said, we just heard from Barkin this week and he didn't offer much in the way of guidance.

One notable recent comment from him was in late September when he said that this cycle could be like the 1990s mid-cycle adjustment. Barkin was comparing now to an easing cycle in the 1990s, when Greenspan cut rates by 75 bps over seven months at the end of 1995. So by that analogue -- if you took it directly -- would be more dovish than what is priced in now. He also said he would not yet make an overheating case, but economy is firming and not weakening and that businesses feel they have pricing power.

I would not put it past him to tip towards the hawkish side but he's usually not the guy to make the first big wave.

Next on the calendar will be Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will appear on Yahoo Finance at 3 pm ET. He's candid but we have heard from him plenty and he has been leaning hawkish for awhile. That said, he hasn't been kicking down the door calling for rate hikes so if we see an incremental move in that direction today, it could be telling.

Tomorrow, we get to hear from the top guy with an 11:30 pm ET 'fireside chat' including Warsh at the IMF meetings. We will see if he sticks to his plan of not giving guidance or lets it out, my guess is that he will have to give a nod in one direction. Earlier that day, we will also hear from Hammack, who has been increasingly hawkish.

The Friday calendar is currently bare of Fed speakers but we will monitor that for any changes.

In terms of economic data, we also get PPI and retail sales tomorrow so those will be key.

titre: Lagarde: no second-round effects yet, but ECB can’t wait until they are in full view
titre_fr: Lagarde: no second-round effects yet, but ECB can’t wait until they are in full view
contenu:
Lagarde’s message leans hawkish at the margin. A central bank that will act on early hints, without waiting for clear evidence of second-round effects, could move sooner than markets expect if wage settlements firm. That supports front-end European yields and the euro on a relative basis. Energy is the key transmission channel. With inflation driven mainly by energy prices, a further jump in oil or gas from Gulf escalation would raise the odds of pre-emptive tightening, making crude and TTF gas direct inputs into ECB pricing. Her comments on France offer no backstop signal, so the French-German yield spread remains exposed to Paris’s budget politics.

-

Lagarde sees no wage-price spiral yet, but she has made clear the ECB will act on the first signs rather than wait for proof.

Summary:

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said the euro area has yet to see second-round effects from higher energy prices, but signalled the central bank would not wait for them to become fully visible before responding.

Lagarde said inflation has been rising predominantly, though not exclusively, as a result of energy prices. While there is no sign yet of those increases feeding through into broader wages and prices, she said policymakers must anticipate and look for early hints. The ECB is paying particular attention to collective bargaining arrangements, where expectations of future wage increases tend to show up first.

Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a jump in energy costs, prompts workers to seek higher wages and companies to raise prices further, turning a temporary spike into more persistent inflation. Lagarde’s emphasis on acting before those effects are fully evident suggests a readiness to respond pre-emptively if wage settlements begin to firm.

On the economy, Lagarde said growth is not brilliant, but that euro area growth of 1.1% in 2026 is not bad.

Asked about France’s debt, she said the primary and first solution lies in French fiscal policy. The remark puts the onus on Paris rather than the ECB as French borrowing costs face pressure. Goldman Sachs noted in a recent client discussion that the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply amid political tensions over the French budget, an issue it expects to persist ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Lagarde, who is French, also said she will not run for president of France.

Her comments leave energy prices and wage negotiations as the key indicators for the ECB’s next steps. A renewed rise in energy costs, or early evidence of stronger pay demands, would increase pressure on policymakers to act before inflation becomes entrenched.

titre: Goldman Sachs says RBA minutes lower bar for November hike, with three hawkish signals
titre_fr: Goldman Sachs says RBA minutes lower bar for November hike, with three hawkish signals
contenu:
Goldman’s read raises the risk that the next RBA move comes sooner than its own base case. That leaves the third-quarter CPI release as the main event for the Australian dollar and short-dated bond yields. The minutes’ emphasis on domestic capacity shifts the focus from energy pass-through to underlying inflation, so even a moderate headline print could carry hawkish weight if services and core measures stay firm. Oil still matters at the margin: the minutes noted that domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and a renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war would strengthen the case for tightening. Market pricing had already leaned toward further hikes before the September decision, so a hot CPI reading could quickly firm up expectations for November.

---

Goldman isn’t calling a November hike yet, but it thinks theRBA minuteshave opened the door, and the CPI report later this month will decide whether the board walks through it.

Summary:

Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s September policy meeting have likely lowered the bar for another interest rate increase in November, according to Goldman Sachs economists. The bank still expects rates to stay on hold.

In a report, three members of Goldman’s economics research team said they viewed the minutes, released on Tuesday, as more hawkish than Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference after the decision, for three reasons. Among them, the economists said the minutes showed increased concern about domestic capacity pressures, with the board treating July’s stronger-than-expected inflation data as evidence of that.

Goldman continues to expect the RBA to hold the cash rate at 4.60% at its next meeting. However, it judged that the minutes have lowered the threshold for a further hike in November, depending on the outcome of the third-quarter consumer price index report.

The minutes support that reading. They showed the board unanimously raised rates by 25 basis points at the 28 to 29 September meeting because several upside risks to inflation flagged in August had either materialised or were building. Those risks included a broader Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher, cost pressures from the global AI boom, and tighter domestic capacity than assumed. Members said excess demand in the economy appeared greater than previously assessed. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation was higher than thought, and business surveys pointed to a drift higher in firms’ inflation expectations.

The board also noted that, if global neutral interest rates have risen, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. It said holding steady while other central banks tightened could loosen Australian financial conditions through a weaker currency. Members concluded that they would remain attentive to incoming data and would raise rates further if required.

The third-quarter CPI report, due on 28 October at 00:30 GMT (20:30 ET on 27 October), now looks pivotal. The RBA’s next decision follows on 3 November at 03:30 GMT (22:30 ET on 2 November), alongside its updated quarterly forecasts. A strong reading on underlying and services inflation would test Goldman’s hold call and could push the board toward a second consecutive increase.

---

If nothing in November the RBA has another crack in December before a long break until the next meeting 8–9 February 2027:

titre: Singapore: MAS could tighten again in 2027 if inflation risks materialise, says ANZ
titre_fr: Singapore: MAS could tighten again in 2027 if inflation risks materialise, says ANZ
contenu:
ANZ’s view tempers any dovish reading of Wednesday’s surprise hold. If markets come to see it as a pause within a tightening cycle, any Singapore dollar weakness against its trading partners could prove limited. The bar for a further move now appears to be evidence that inflation risks are materialising, which puts imported energy costs at the centre of the outlook. A renewed surge in oil or refined product prices tied to Gulf escalation would be the most likely trigger for MAS to steepen the slope of its policy band again. Easing in crude would strengthen the case for an extended hold.

--

ANZ reads the MAS hold as a breather, not a turning point: the earlier tightenings need time to work, but the door to more remains open.

Summary:

The Monetary Authority of Singapore could resume tightening next year if upside risks to inflation materialise, according to ANZ, one of the few forecasters that correctly predicted the central bank would leave policy unchanged on Wednesday.

Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, said MAS judged there was no need to tighten further at this stage because the effects of its two earlier tightening moves, in April and July, are still feeding through the economy. Monetary policy works with a lag, and changes to the path of the Singapore dollar take time to show up in import prices and, in turn, consumer inflation.

That was despite a stronger economic backdrop than expected. Goh noted that third-quarter GDP growth beat expectations and that MAS still expects core inflation to remain slightly elevated in the near term. He stressed, however, that the decision does not signal the end of the tightening cycle, and that MAS could tighten again if upside inflation risks emerge next year.

titre: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
titre_fr: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
contenu:
How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers

Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners’ currencies. When MAS “tightens,” it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it “eases,” it slows or reverses that appreciation.

That is whyWednesday’s decision to hold policy steadywas framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate.

Why Singapore uses the exchange rate

Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates.

There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US.

What is the S$NEER?

The S$NEER, or Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, measures the Singapore dollar against a weighted basket of the currencies of Singapore's main trading partners. MAS does not publish the basket's composition or weights. It manages the S$NEER within a policy band, stepping into the currency market when needed to keep it there.

The three levers

MAS adjusts policy through three features of the band, none of which it discloses precisely.

Analysts estimate the band’s width and slope from the currency’s movements, but MAS keeps the exact parameters private. That gives it room to act without inviting speculation against fixed levels.

How often MAS decides

MAS reviews policy four times a year, in January, April, July and October, having moved from a twice-yearly schedule in 2024. Decisions are released early in the Singapore morning, which is around midnight GMT.

The inflation measure that matters

MAS focuses on core inflation, which excludes accommodation and private transport costs. Those categories are heavily influenced by government policy and housing and car-ownership cycles, so stripping them out gives a cleaner read on underlying price pressures. On Wednesday, MAS forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027.

What Wednesday’s decision means

By leaving all three levers unchanged, MAS kept the Singapore dollar on its existing appreciating path. That is still a restraint on imported inflation, just not an increased one. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected a tightening, most likely through a steeper slope, so the hold was a dovish surprise relative to expectations, even though the policy setting itself remains a tightening bias.

Key takeaway for traders

When reading an MAS statement, watch for the words “slope,” “width” and “centre.” Any change to them is the policy decision. For the Singapore dollar, the slope sets the medium-term direction against the basket, while a re-centring can produce a sharp immediate move. Because Singapore’s inflation is so sensitive to import costs, especially energy, oil prices are often a better guide to the next MAS move than local interest rates.

titre: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
titre_fr: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
contenu:
The decision is a dovish surprise against a unanimous call for tightening, which leaves the Singapore dollar vulnerable to some softening against its trading partners as positions built for a hawkish move unwind. The policy band still has an appreciating slope, though, so this is a pause in tightening, not an easing. Energy is the key swing factor. MAS explicitly flagged a sharp, sustained surge in energy prices as an upside risk, so a renewed jump in crude tied to Gulf escalation would put tightening firmly back on the table at the next review. Singapore’s position as a regional oil-trading and refining hub makes its imported inflation particularly sensitive to oil and refined product prices.

--

MAS chose patience over pre-emption, betting that slightly elevated inflation will ease on its own as the AI boom cools and import costs fade.

Summary:

The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept its monetary policy settings unchanged on Wednesday, defying expectations for a tightening as it judged that slightly elevated inflation should ease over time.

The central bank, which manages policy through the exchange rate, said it would maintain the current rate of appreciation of its policy band, known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate or S$NEER. There will be no change to the width of the band or the level at which it is centred. The band is already on an appreciating path, which helps restrain imported inflation, so the decision leaves that tightening bias in place without adding to it. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten.

MAS said the economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, but moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten. It expects AI-related activity to slow in the second half of 2027 and the economy’s positive output gap, a sign that demand is running ahead of capacity, to narrow through next year. The government will announce its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 in November.

On prices, MAS expects firming imported cost pressures to keep both core and headline inflation at their current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead. Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 as a whole, before easing more discernibly from the middle of next year as import costs ebb.

The central bank stressed that significant uncertainty surrounds the outlook and that, for now, risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than forecast. On the other hand, a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates or a sharper pullback in AI-related investment could drag on growth and, in turn, inflation.

The hold suggests MAS is prepared to look through near-term price pressures on the view that they will fade, while keeping its appreciating policy stance in place. With risks still skewed to the upside, the path of energy prices and the strength of the AI cycle are likely to shape whether it moves at its next review.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the coutnry's central bank.

---

titre: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
titre_fr: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
contenu:
With October largely priced out, Tuesday’s trio keeps December in focus for the next move.Williams’ commentson 2027 cap how far markets can push expectations for the peak rate. That should limit the upside for longer-dated Treasury yields and the dollar unless the data turns. Barkin’s warning that shocks are continuing gives the hawkish camp an opening if inflation stays sticky. Oil is the swing factor. Williams’ benign outlook assumes energy won’t add to inflation next year, so a renewed crude surge, for example from escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites, would undercut that view and strengthen the case for more tightening. For now, oil is effectively a direct input into Fed pricing.

---Three Fed voices agree the inflation fight isn’t over; the open question is whether today’s shocks fade on their own or keep the Fed hiking into 2027.

Summary:

Three Federal Reserve officials on Tuesday signalled that the fight against inflation is not over, with two backing one more interest rate increase this year, though New York Fed President John Williams suggested the tightening cycle may end there.

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, speaking at Howard University, said the Fed’s 2% inflation target is not out of reach and can be achieved. He said it is clear that inflation is proving enduring and that shocks to prices are continuing, making it sensible for the Fed to act. Barkin, who does not vote on policy this year, also said policymakers can see the effect of artificial intelligence investment on US inflation.

Williams, who is vice chair of the Fed’s rate-setting committee, told Bloomberg News he had not changed his view that one more rate hike may be appropriate in 2026. He said he currently sees no reason to believe the Fed would need to do more in 2027, though the outlook could change and policymakers must keep watching the data. Williams expects inflation to fall substantially next year to near 2% for 2027 as a whole, as tariff effects fade completely and energy prices stop adding to inflation. He acknowledged that high energy prices tied to the Middle East war and tech-related investment are lifting near-term pressures, but argued the economy is not overheating.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins struck a firmer tone. In prepared remarks, [she said she expects the Fed to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year] and described the risk of high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus. She expects headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months because of higher prices for diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. In [follow-up comments, Collins said economic uncertainty is elevated] and that she is watching how broad-based inflation pressures are.

Together, the comments point to a Fed that agrees on the near-term direction but is split on the nature of the problem. Williams sees inflation driven by specific shocks that should fade, while Barkin’s emphasis on continuing shocks and Collins’ focus on the breadth of price pressures point to a risk that inflation proves more persistent.

The Fed raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% in September. Williams’ comments late that month led markets to largely price out a hike at the October 27-28 meeting, leaving December as the more likely timing for the next move.

titre: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
titre_fr: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
contenu:
Collins’ focus on how widespread inflation is moves attention to core and services prices, not just the headline energy-driven numbers. Signs of fuel costs spreading into broader prices would firm December hike pricing and support front-end yields and the dollar. For oil, that means sustained strength in crude and products now carries a second-round risk the Fed is explicitly watching. Her stress on elevated uncertainty also leaves room for the data to delay the next move, which caps how aggressively markets can price an October hike.

---

Collins has already called for another hike, and now she is spelling out what will set the timing: whether inflation spreads beyond energy in an uncertain economy.

Summary:

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday that economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is paying close attention to how broad-based inflation pressures are, as she set out the factors that will shape her view on the timing of the next rate move.

Collins said she is very focused on the inflation data and that she looks at the economy holistically when weighing the future path of policy. Her emphasis on breadth suggests she will be watching whether price pressures spread into a wider range of goods and services, rather than staying concentrated in a few categories.

The comments add detailto remarks earlier in the dayin which [Collins said she expects the Fed to raise rates again before the end of 2026]. In that speech text, prepared for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, she said she had supported the central bank’s quarter-point hike in September, which took the policy rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, and called the risk of high inflation the Fed’s main focus.

Collins has flagged several forces that could keep inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, including investment in data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure, the ongoing effect of tariffs, and energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She has said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months, citing recent increases in prices for refined fuels such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil.

Her baseline outlook remains constructive, with healthy growth, a job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to target. Her latest comments make clear, however, that she sees the outlook as uncertain and that the incoming data will decide how quickly she wants policy to move.

Policymaker projections released in September pointed to one more increase this year. Several Fed officials have suggested in recent weeks that it is more likely in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins has said the policy path into the new year will depend on the data.

contenu:

That should keep front-end Treasury yields supported and limit room for a sustained dollar pullback while hikes stay in play. Collins sees a resilient economy as giving the Fed licence to keep tightening, with war-driven fuel costs the clearest reason inflation won’t get back to target on its own.

Summary:

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday she expects the US central bank will need to lift interest rates again before the end of 2026, arguing that further tightening is needed to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target in a timely and lasting way.

In prepared remarks for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, reported by Reuters, Collins said she had supported the Federal Open Market Committee’s decision last month to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. She indicated that a modest additional increase would likely be appropriate this year, while stressing that her view on both the need for and timing of further action would rest on the full body of incoming data and how it shapes the balance of risks.

titre: BoE’s Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
titre_fr: BoE’s Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
contenu:
Greene’s remarks reinforce the hawkish wing of the MPC and support market expectations of a November hike, which recent reports put at around 84%. Her warning about second-round effects ties directly to the energy shock from the Iran war: if higher oil and diesel costs feed into wages and pricing, the case for tightening strengthens further, keeping short-dated gilt yields and sterling sensitive to energy prices. The comments also add pressure on the gilt market at a time when global bond yields are already elevated. Upcoming UK wage and inflation data will be key for whether her view gains wider support on the committee.

--Greene’s message is simple: by the time inflation shows up in wages and prices, it will be too late, so the Bank should move before it gets there.

Summary:

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene said UK monetary policy is not that restrictive, warning that waiting for second-round inflation effects to become visible before acting would leave the central bank responding too late.

Greene, an external member of the Monetary Policy Committee, said she sees the bigger risk as failing to be proactive enough in tackling inflation, rather than raising interest rates too soon. Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a rise in energy costs, feeds into wages and broader price-setting, making inflation more persistent.

Her comments reinforce her position as one of the more hawkish members of the committee. Greene voted for a quarter-point rate increase at the Bank’s July and September meetings, when she was among three members outvoted by a majority that preferred to keep rates on hold.

Greene has made similar arguments in recent days. Last week, she said she expected the UK to see some second-round effects from the current inflation cycle and voiced concern that wage growth of around 3.5% next year would be worrying, raising the risk that higher prices feed into pay deals and prompt firms to raise prices further.

She said the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts for the UK did not surprise her. The IMF raised its 2026 UK growth forecast to 1.3% this week, citing stronger AI-related investment, while warning that the global outlook faces significant risks from the war in the Middle East and elevated energy prices.

The UK, like other major economies, is grappling with inflation pressure from higher oil and diesel prices following the conflict involving Iran. Policymakers who favour acting early argue that letting those costs become embedded in wages and inflation expectations would ultimately require more painful tightening later.

Markets have increasingly priced a rate hike at the Bank’s November meeting, and Greene’s remarks suggest she will continue to make the case for tighter policy. The next round of UK wage and inflation data will help determine whether that view gains broader support on the committee.

titre: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
titre_fr: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
contenu:
The minutes read hawkish,not unexpectedly,with the board explicitly keeping further hikes on the table and markets already pricing roughly another 15 basis points by year-end and 30 basis points in the first half of 2027. Oil is central to the outlook: domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and any further escalation of the Iran war would feed directly into the risk of more tightening. The board’s concern that a lagging RBA could weaken the Australian dollar suggests it is willing to keep pace with other central banks, which should support the currency against a backdrop of rising global yields. Rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, property and consumer discretionary remain vulnerable, given falling house prices and the board’s view that household spending must stay subdued for some time.

---

The RBA has concluded the economy is running hotter and the neutral rate is higher than it thought, which is central bank language for “we may not be done yet”.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates last month because several of the upside risks to inflation it had flagged in August had either materialised or were building, according to minutes of the 28 to 29 September meeting released on Tuesday. The board signalled it was prepared to tighten further if needed.

The board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%. Members said the August forecasts, which had inflation returning to the midpoint of the target range by around late 2027, depended on a series of favourable developments that no longer looked likely to all occur.

The minutes set out three main arguments for the move. First, the risks identified in August had largely come to pass. The Middle East conflict had broadened and oil prices were well above the level assumed in the forecasts, with domestic petrol and diesel prices running about 13% higher than projected. Global cost pressures were intensifying, driven partly by extraordinary demand for AI-related products, and domestic capacity appeared tighter than assessed. Second, members judged that responding quickly would best balance their inflation and employment goals, given inflation has been above target for an extended period and surveys point to a risk that business inflation expectations are rising. Third, the board said the cash rate might not be high enough to restore balance within a reasonable timeframe even if the risks did not fully materialise.

That last point reflected a significant shift in thinking about the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Members said that if market signals of a higher global neutral rate were correct, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. They added that if the RBA held still while other central banks tightened, Australian financial conditions could loosen through a weaker currency.

On the economy, the board noted June quarter growth was a little stronger than expected, driven by business investment that rose more than 10% over the year, partly reflecting data centre and renewable energy construction. Household consumption slowed to a below-trend pace, house prices fell faster than expected, and unemployment rose to 4.6% in August. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation is higher than previously thought, which would mean more pressure on capacity than estimated. Unit labour cost growth, driven by weak productivity rather than strong wages, also remained above levels consistent with the target.

Members acknowledged the trade-off between inflation and employment had worsened because of global cost pressures, and said returning inflation to target would require accepting slower growth in demand and jobs. The board will remain attentive to incoming data and said it will do what is necessary, including increasing the cash rate further if required.

titre: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6981 – Reuters estimate
titre_fr: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6981 – Reuters estimate
contenu:
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.

---

Earlier:

---

The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.

Summary:

The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.

That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.

September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.

The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

titre: Fed’s Hammack says more tightening needed to cool demand, keeps open mind on pace
titre_fr: Fed’s Hammack says more tightening needed to cool demand, keeps open mind on pace
contenu:
Hammack’s remarks reinforce the hawkish tilt within the Fed and keep the possibility of a back-to-back hike alive, even though markets currently expect a hold in October. Her explicit focus on AI-driven capex and wealth effects puts high-flying tech equities in the crosshairs, since tighter policy aimed at curbing investment and asset-fuelled spending works partly through valuations. The comments should lend support to the dollar and front-end Treasury yields, while also weighing on gold, which has tended to fall as rate hike expectations build. Traders will watch whether other voters echo her view that the inflation fight now targets demand directly rather than the labour market.

---

Hammack wants to take some heat out of a booming economy without burning the labour market, and she is open about which part of demand she would prefer to cool first.

Summary:

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said on Monday she believes US interest rates need to rise further to restrain demand. She also said she hopes the Fed can bring inflation down without damaging a labour market that remains close to full employment.

In an interview with Reuters, Hammack said demand is being driven both by a rapid pace of corporate investment and by market-driven wealth gains that are supporting consumer spending, factors she sees as keeping inflation lodged in a range of 2.5% to 3.0%. In her view, restrictive monetary policy could cool those forces enough for inflation to fall without unemployment rising beyond the current 4.2%. She said she is not trying to stop growth, only to slow it to a pace that eases pricing pressure. A pullback in either business investment or consumption would help, she added, and restraint on the capital spending side might mean less of the burden falls on consumers.

titre: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
titre_fr: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
contenu:
The People’s Bank of China publishes its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time the previous evening), and the number has become one of the most closely followed signals in Asian currency markets. Its importance has grown over the past month as Beijing has moved from holding back the yuan’s rise to steering it gradually higher.

---

Earlier:

---

Under China’s managed float, the onshore yuan may trade up to 2% either side of the midpoint set each morning. The central bank arrives at that midpoint by weighing the previous session’s close, moves in the US dollar and other major currencies, wider global FX conditions, and domestic priorities including capital flows, growth and financial stability. Because the calculation leaves room for judgement, the fixing doubles as a tool for shaping expectations.

Once the rate is published, onshore trading proceeds within the band. If pressure drives the yuan toward either limit, the PBOC can respond by buying or selling the currency directly, adjusting liquidity, or acting through state-owned banks. That is why markets treat the fixing as a statement of intent. A midpoint stronger than forecast usually signals resistance to depreciation, while a weaker one can point to acceptance of a softer yuan, or discomfort with how quickly it is gaining.

For close to a year, the second message prevailed. The PBOC consistently set the midpoint weaker than market forecasts, which traders took as an effort to slow appreciation. That gap was at its widest since February in late August, soon after the yuan hit a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.

September marked a turning point. The central bank lifted the fixing for eight sessions in a row, its longest run since 2023, taking the midpoint to its strongest since February 2023. The onshore yuan climbed to levels last seen in January 2023 and the offshore rate to its firmest since July 2022. Yet the fixing is still being set well below estimates, at one point by more than 500 pips against a Reuters survey, suggesting Beijing is easing the brakes rather than releasing them.

Goldman Sachs analysts tied the firmer fixings to the run-up to the recent Trump-Xi summit, a pattern they said matches past diplomacy, and expect policymakers to remain comfortable with steady, gradual gains.

The trade-off has not changed. A stronger yuan supports capital stability and lowers import costs, but rapid gains could hurt exporters while the domestic economy remains soft. The daily gap between the fixing and consensus forecasts remains the clearest guide to how far Beijing will let the yuan run, and whether that tolerance outlasts the summit

titre: ECB president Lagarde talks of 'unwarranted' market moves, but who gets to decide what is warranted?
titre_fr: ECB president Lagarde talks of 'unwarranted' market moves, but who gets to decide what is warranted?
contenu:
Ah, here we go again. Just when you think that the bond market is finally starting to hold governments accountable for their fiscal decisions, along comes the ECB with a reminder to everyone that it has tools to come to the rescue. How convenient.

ECB president Lagarde remarked yesterday that the central bank has the necessary tools to counter "unwarranted" market dynamics, in what surely is a reference to the ongoing turmoil in European bond markets.

Now, I don't have a problem with the ECB stepping in when markets genuinely become dysfunctional. However, there is one thing that really bothers me about her statement. What exactly constitutes to an "unwarranted" market move in this particular case?

Well, it is not difficult to draw a connection with what is happening in France right now. The country is running a budget deficit of more than 5% of GDP and public debt is approaching 120% of GDP. Meanwhile, a political gridlock is stopping any meaningful fiscal reform from taking place.

So if investors are demanding higher yields in order to compensate for those risks, isn't that just the bond market doing its job? Pfft. I mean, at what point does a reasonable repricing of fiscal risk suddenly become something that warrants central bank intervention? Where does one actually draw the line on that? And better yet, who exactly gets to decide where that line should be drawn?

The ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) is designed to address disorderly market conditions that threaten monetary policy transmission. It is not meant to provide governments with a convenient escape route from their own fiscal problems.

As such, France's ongoing excessive deficit procedure raises questions over whether it would even qualify for intervention under the ECB's existing framework. And I would argue that is exactly the reason why Lagarde's choice of words deserves scrutiny here.

The ECB should be staying in their lane and focus on the mandate of delivering on price stability, not to shield governments from the consequences of poor fiscal choices. If intervention starts to border on the lines of being a backdoor bailout, then the distinction between monetary policy and fiscal support becomes rather blurred. And that is quite a dangerous precedence to set.

Just think about it. If politicians know that the ECB will eventually ride to the rescue whenever borrowing costs become too painful, then where is the incentive to make those difficult fiscal decisions in the first place?

Let's be real. The bond market isn't necessarily broken just because governments don't like what investors are telling them.

titre: Fed's Waller says more hikes are needed but can be flexible about the pace, downplays September NFP weakness
titre_fr: Fed's Waller says more hikes are needed but can be flexible about the pace, downplays September NFP weakness
contenu:
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said that additional rate hikes will likely be needed to bring inflation back to the Fed’s 2% target, although he added that the pace of tightening can remain flexible. Speaking at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye’s Istanbul Economic Forum, Waller said further hikes do not necessarily need to come at consecutive meetings, leaving the door open to a pause at the Fed’s October 27–28 meeting. If the economy and inflation evolve as expected, however, he anticipates additional increases will eventually be required.

Waller's main concern remains persistent inflation and the risk that it becomes embedded in expectations. He noted that inflation has now been above the Fed’s 2% target for around five and a half years, while the economy appears to have strengthened in the second half of 2026. He highlighted several persistent inflationary forces, including the ongoing energy shock linked to the Iran conflict and rising demand associated with the AI buildout. At the same time, he described the labor market as “solid and stable” despite the slowdown in job creation in September, suggesting that the Fed has room to keep its focus firmly on inflation without being overly concerned about causing a damaging economic slowdown. Yesterday'sFOMC minutessimilarly showed concern that energy costs and AI-related investment could keep inflation pressures elevated.

Waller also addressed the Fed’s approach to forward guidance and communication. Rather than committing to a predetermined rate path, he argued that policymakers can still signal the range of policy choices they are considering while retaining flexibility to respond to incoming data. In his view, this allows markets to form expectations about the likely direction of policy without the Fed making promises it may later have to reverse.

The market reaction to his remarks has been relatively muted so far, as a pause in October has been already priced in after Fed's Williams and Fed's Jefferson push back, as well as the softer than expected NFP report. Right now, the market is pricing just a 20% chance of a rate hike in October as the US CPI data next week could still move the needle. Looking ahead, traders are expecting at least three more rate hikes by the end of 2027, taking the FFR range to 4.50-4.75%.

titre: Japan's answer to FedWatch: TFX launches BoJ meeting-by-meeting rate futures
titre_fr: Japan's answer to FedWatch: TFX launches BoJ meeting-by-meeting rate futures
contenu:
A liquid meeting-by-meeting contract would give the yen market something it has lacked: a clear, quotable read on the odds of a BoJ hike at each decision. That could make yen moves around BoJ meetings more orderly, as surprises get priced earlier, while sharpening reactions to data and official comments between meetings. Easier hedging of short-term rate risk may also support activity in front-end Japanese government bonds and yen carry trades, where the cost of being caught out by a hike has risen. Liquidity is the key test: a thinly traded contract will produce noisy signals rather than reliable odds.

---

Japan is finally getting its own version of the tool Wall Street uses to bet on Fed decisions, and the BoJ's quickening hiking cycle is the reason.

Summary:

Japan is set to get a sharper tool for betting on Bank of Japan decisions, as the Tokyo Financial Exchange prepares to launch futures that let traders position for rate moves at individual policy meetings.

The new contract, due to launch this month, is linked to the Tokyo Overnight Average Rate (TONA), the uncollateralised overnight rate at which banks lend to each other and which the BoJ targets with its policy. It is designed to let traders hedge or take positions on rate changes in the window between two BoJ meetings, according to reports citing the exchange.

The move responds to a change in how the BoJ operates. The central bank raised interest rates to a 31-year high last month, and Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled a new phase aimed at preventing inflation from overshooting its target, leaving the door open to further increases. When a central bank is on hold, investors have little need to price each meeting separately. Once it is actively hiking, every decision becomes a live event that traders want to hedge.

TFX said its existing three-month TONA futures had failed to meet that need, because they do not isolate the outcome of a single meeting. A director in the exchange's wholesale business said rate volatility has increased and demand for derivatives is rising.

The trading figures point to the gap. Despite broad expectations of further BoJ tightening, volume in the three-month contract has fallen in recent months, with September activity down nearly 50% from a year earlier. That suggests traders are hedging BoJ risk through other instruments rather than abandoning it.

The comparison with the US is instructive. Fed funds futures underpin widely quoted measures of the probability of Fed rate moves at each meeting, which have become a standard reference for markets and media alike. A liquid meeting-based TONA contract could in time offer something similar for the BoJ, giving yen traders a clearer, real-time read on hike odds.

Whether it does will depend on uptake. The first test is how much volume the contract attracts around the next BoJ decisions, and whether its pricing proves a reliable guide to what the central bank actually does.

titre: NY Fed survey: US one-year inflation expectations jump to 3.9%, highest since May 2023
titre_fr: NY Fed survey: US one-year inflation expectations jump to 3.9%, highest since May 2023
contenu:
The jump in near-term expectations lands squarely on the Fed's main stated worry and strengthens the case for another hike before year end, supporting front-end Treasury yields and the dollar. Rising expected gasoline price growth shows how energy costs are feeding household inflation psychology, which makes oil supply disruptions a more direct risk to the Fed outlook. Stable five-year expectations limit the alarm for longer-dated bonds for now. Consumers also turned less bullish on equities, with fewer expecting stock prices to be higher in a year.

---

Earlier:

---

American households now expect prices to rise half as fast again as their pay over the coming year, the kind of gap that keeps the Fed leaning towards higher rates.

Summary:

US consumers' expectations for inflation over the next year rose to their highest level in more than three years in September, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York'sSurvey of Consumer Expectationsreleased on Wednesday.

Median one-year-ahead inflation expectations increased by 0.3 percentage point to 3.9%, the highest reading since May 2023, while the three-year measure rose 0.1 point to 3.3%. Five-year expectations were unchanged at 3.0%. Disagreement among respondents widened at all horizons, and uncertainty about inflation increased over one and three years.

The rise was broad across household costs. Expected price growth increased for gasoline to 4.8%, food to 5.5%, medical care to 9.2%, rent to 6.8% and college costs to 7.5%, the last a jump of 1.4 points in a single month.

The survey points to a squeeze on household budgets. Expected earnings growth fell 0.3 point to 2.6%, well below expected inflation, yet households anticipate lifting their spending by 5.5% over the coming year, the highest since May 2023. Respondents reported a worse financial situation than a year ago and expect conditions to deteriorate further. They also saw credit as harder to obtain, although the perceived chance of missing a minimum debt payment fell to 12.2%.

Labour market expectations improved. The perceived probability of losing one's job in the next year fell to 13.5%, the lowest since December 2024, while expectations of finding a new job and of quitting voluntarily both rose. The share expecting higher unemployment a year from now eased to 43.9%.

The release arrived hours before minutes of the Fed's September meeting, which showed officials unanimously backed a quarter-point hike to 3.75-4%, with most judging another increase likely by year end. Several officials in the minutes noted elevated short-term inflation expectations, and some warned that more than five years of above-target inflation could begin to influence expectations and wage and price decisions. One-year expectations have climbed from 3.0% in February, so September's reading gives that concern more weight.

The stability of five-year expectations remains the Fed's key reassurance. Whether that anchor holds as energy prices stay high will be central to the debate at the 27-28 October policy meeting.

New York Fed.

titre: ICYMI: Fed minutes: most officials see another hike by year end after unanimous rise to 3.75-4%
titre_fr: ICYMI: Fed minutes: most officials see another hike by year end after unanimous rise to 3.75-4%
contenu:
The minutes back a hawkish read of the Fed path, keeping a further hike at the 27-28 October meeting or in December firmly in play and supporting front-end Treasury yields. The explicit link between prolonged high energy prices and broader inflation makes oil a direct input into Fed pricing: further supply shocks in the Gulf would likely strengthen the case for additional tightening rather than be looked through. For the dollar, the hawkish tone is partly offset by tightening abroad, with the ECB also raising rates, which has narrowed rate differentials. Equity investors may take some comfort that officials see financial conditions as still supportive of growth.

--

Earlier:

---

The Fed didn't just raise rates in September; most of its policymakers were already pencilling in another hike before the year is out, with oil and the AI boom keeping them wary of inflation.

Summary:

Federal Reserve policymakers unanimously supported raising interest rates in September, and most of them judged that another increase would likely be appropriate before the end of the year, according to minutes of the 15-16 September meeting released on Wednesday at 2pm US Eastern time (1800 GMT).

The Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to lift the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75-4%. Participants pointed to inflation that remained elevated, a labour market close to full employment with some signs of strengthening, and solid economic growth. Almost all judged that while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to employment had faded and were now broadly balanced.

Officials said they had not seen enough progress on bringing inflation down in recent months. They cited geopolitical developments that had pushed up crude oil and refined fuel prices, alongside a surge in AI-related investment, as key sources of pressure. Many participants warned that the longer energy prices stayed high, the greater the risk that cost increases in specific sectors would spread into broader price pressures. Some voiced concern that more than five years of above-target inflation could begin to affect expectations and wage and price setting.

Fed staff estimated that the headline personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% in the year to August, with the core measure at 3.4%. Staff raised their inflation forecasts for 2026 through 2028 and projected inflation would not reach the 2% goal until 2029.

Opinions differed on the rationale for tightening. Many participants saw a higher rate path as prudent insurance against persistent inflation, while a number viewed it as necessary based on their central economic outlook. A couple said they had raised their estimates of the neutral interest rate, and several suggested that policy was not restrictive, or only mildly so, even after the hike.

On the economy, officials noted that the scale and pace of the AI buildout had continued to surprise to the upside and was boosting business investment. Several observed that stock market gains were supporting spending by higher-income households, while lower and middle-income households were being squeezed by higher energy costs.

Looking ahead, participants said they would approach each meeting with an open mind. The committee next meets on 27-28 October, when incoming inflation data and energy market developments will shape whether the next hike comes sooner or later.

Federal Reserve Chair Warsh
contenu_fr:
The minutes back a hawkish read of the Fed path, keeping a further hike at the 27-28 October meeting or in December firmly in play and supporting front-end Treasury yields. The explicit link between prolonged high energy prices and broader inflation makes oil a direct input into Fed pricing: further supply shocks in the Gulf would likely strengthen the case for additional tightening rather than be looked through. For the dollar, the hawkish tone is partly offset by tightening abroad, with the ECB also raising rates, which has narrowed rate differentials. Equity investors may take some comfort that officials see financial conditions as still supportive of growth.

titre: RBI decision today: most economists expect a hike to 5.50%, MUFG sees a hold
titre_fr: RBI decision today: most economists expect a hike to 5.50%, MUFG sees a hold
contenu:
Oil is the common thread in every forecast. India imports most of its crude, so prices above $100 a barrel feed straight into inflation and the trade deficit, while higher US yields pull capital out of emerging markets and weigh on the rupee. A hike today would be largely expected, so the reaction is likely to turn on guidance: signals of a second move in December would support the rupee and push short-dated government bond yields higher. A hold, asMUFG expects, would be the bigger surprise and could weaken the rupee in the near term, although the RBI's large reserves give it room to lean against any sharp fall. Any announcement on draining surplus liquidity would act as a tightening in its own right, whatever happens to the repo rate.

----

The debate over the Reserve Bank of India is no longer whether it tightens but when, with most economists saying today and MUFG saying December.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of India is expected to raise interest rates for the first time in more than three years when it announces its policy decision today, although forecasters are split on timing, with MUFG standing apart from the consensus in predicting a hold.

The six-member Monetary Policy Committee will announce its decision at 10:00 am India time (04:30 GMT, 00:30 ET). The repo rate has been held at 5.25% for four straight meetings, following 125 basis points of cuts in 2025.

A Reuters poll published on 28 September found that 35 of 61 economists expect a 25 basis point increase to 5.50% today, which would be the RBI's first hike since February 2023. More than half of those who gave a longer-term view expect at least one further increase by December. Nomura is among those forecasting back-to-back moves, with hikes today and in December taking the repo rate to 5.75%. Economists at India's largest lender said the balance of risks had tilted decisively toward a hike, citing broadening inflation, a worsening global backdrop and renewed repricing of risk in financial markets.

MUFG takes a different view on timing. It expects the RBI to hold today but sees the pause as temporary, forecasting 25 basis point hikes in December and February, with some risk of 75 basis points in total across the cycle. The bank cites higher oil prices, weather-related risks, resilient domestic demand and plentiful banking system liquidity as factors likely to keep price pressures elevated into 2027. It also says rising US yields are putting pressure on the rupee, although the RBI has ample reserves to defend the currency. Even its full forecast would amount to less tightening than rates markets are currently pricing, MUFG said.

The split is about when, not whether. Both camps point to the same drivers: crude oil above $100 a barrel as a result of the Middle East conflict, inflation that has moved back above the RBI's 4% target, and a global environment in which central banks in the US, UK and Japan have already raised rates.

Beyond the headline decision, investors will watch for any change to the RBI's neutral stance, revisions to its inflation and growth forecasts, comments on the rupee, and possible steps to absorb surplus liquidity. The next policy meeting concludes on 4 December.

titre: RBI expected to hold at 5.25% today, MUFG sees two hikes by February
titre_fr: RBI expected to hold at 5.25% today, MUFG sees two hikes by February
contenu:
Oil is the main channel through which the Middle East conflict reaches Indian policy. As a large net importer of crude, India sees higher energy prices feed quickly into both inflation and the trade balance, adding pressure on the rupee at the same time as rising US yields draw capital away from emerging markets. That makes the RBI's language on currency defence and inflation forecasts as important as the rate decision itself. MUFG's view that markets are already pricing more tightening than it expects suggests a hold without a sharply hawkish signal could support Indian government bonds. A shift away from the neutral stance, or explicit warnings on oil-driven inflation, would push the other way and could lend some support to the rupee.

---

The Reserve Bank of India is expected to stand still today, but MUFG thinks it is only catching its breath before a tightening cycle driven by oil, liquidity and a pressured rupee.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of India is expected to keep its key interest rate unchanged when it announces its policy decision today, but MUFG says the pause is likely to be temporary as inflation risks build.

The decision from the six-member Monetary Policy Committee is due at 10:00 am India time (04:30 GMT, 00:30 ET), at the end of a three-day meeting. The repo rate has been held at 5.25% since February, with the RBI keeping a neutral policy stance at its August review.

MUFG expects another hold today. However, it says recent developments have strengthened its view that the central bank is close to the start of a gradual tightening cycle. Higher oil prices and weather-related risks have raised upside pressure on inflation. Resilient domestic demand and plentiful liquidity in the banking system are likely to keep underlying price pressures elevated into 2027, according to the bank.

Global conditions add to the challenge. Rising US Treasury yields have put pressure on the rupee by drawing capital toward higher returns in the US, although MUFG notes that the RBI has ample reserves to defend the currency against excessive weakness.

The bank forecasts 25 basis point increases at the RBI's December and February meetings, with some risk that the cycle extends to 75 basis points in total. Even that, it says, would be less tightening than rates markets are currently pricing for the cycle as a whole.

Beyond the rate decision, investors will focus on whether the RBI adjusts its neutral stance, how it revises its inflation and growth forecasts in light of higher energy costs, and what it says about liquidity conditions and the rupee. Any signal that policymakers share MUFG's view of building inflation risks would increase expectations for a hike at the next meeting, which concludes on 4 December.

titre: Japan media reports: BOJ's Sato, one of two September dissenters, backs gradual rate hikes
titre_fr: Japan media reports: BOJ's Sato, one of two September dissenters, backs gradual rate hikes
contenu:
Sato's remarks soften the picture of a hardening dovish bloc that unsettled the yen after September's split vote. When one of the board's most reluctant members accepts that policy is still accommodative, the hurdle for the next hike looks lower, even if timing remains open. The oil link matters most. As a major crude importer, Japan feels Middle East supply disruption directly through import costs, and a dove citing that pressure suggests energy prices are now shaping the policy debate across the whole board. Her rejection of a pre-set pace leaves room to argue for delay, so the yen's response is likely to depend on whether other board members echo the gradual-but-onward message.

---

Earlier:

---

The Bank of Japan's newest dove has signalled she is not against hiking, only against hurrying, and Middle East oil is doing much of the persuading.

Summary:

Bank of Japan board member Ayano Sato said she supports raising interest rates in several stages as financial conditions remain accommodative, Kyodo News reported on Wednesday. Her comments suggest that one of the board's two September dissenters is not opposed to further tightening, only to a fixed timetable.

Sato said she agrees on the need for gradual adjustment to interest rates but does not think there should be a pre-set pace for hikes, according to Kyodo. She said risks to the price outlook are skewed somewhat to the upside because of rising oil costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East. She added that the BOJ must decide monetary policy independently while remaining consistent with the government's proactive fiscal policy.

The remarks stand out given Sato's record. Appointed to the board in June under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who is known for her caution over rapid rate increases, Sato was regarded as an advocate of loose policy. At the September meeting, she and fellow Takaichi appointee Toichiro Asada voted against the BOJ's decision to lift its policy rate to 1.25% from 1%. Sato argued at the time that it was not yet the right moment to raise rates.

That 7-2 vote took the policy rate to its highest level since 1995, in the shortest interval between hikes under Governor Kazuo Ueda. The yen weakened on the decision as investors read the two dissents as a possible brake on further tightening.

Sato's comments complicate that interpretation. Her description of financial conditions as accommodative aligns with the BOJ's broader view that real interest rates remain deeply negative, and her concern about oil-driven inflation echoes the bank's earlier warnings about price risks from energy costs and a weak yen. Her objection now appears to be about pace rather than direction.

Analysts polled by Reuters after the September meeting expected the policy rate to reach 1.5% by the end of March and 1.75% in the second quarter of 2027. Sato's remarks do not change that path, but they make it less likely that the dovish members of the board would stand firmly in its way.

titre: RBA papers show a 20% AI stock slump could cut Australian spending by about 2.5%
titre_fr: RBA papers show a 20% AI stock slump could cut Australian spending by about 2.5%
contenu:
The papers cut both ways for rates. Model estimates putting the NAIRU near 5%, above the current 4.6% jobless rate, imply the labour market may still be tighter than the RBA's working assumption, which supports the case for a further hike. The neutral rate range adds to that. With the cash rate at 4.6% and headline inflation at 4%, the rough real policy rate sits inside the RBA's estimated neutral band, a simple calculation that suggests policy may be less restrictive than it looks. Against that, the combined drag from falling house prices and a possible AI-led equity correction points to downside risks to consumption, which would argue for caution. For the Australian dollar and short-end rates, the balance probably keeps November in play while making the decision more data-dependent.

---

The RBA has quietly modelled what an AI bubble bursting would do to Australian spending, and the answer is uncomfortable for a household sector already losing ground on housing.

Summary:

Australian households are more exposed to a downturn in artificial intelligence stocks than their direct shareholdings suggest, and a sharp correction could feed through to consumer spending, according to internal Reserve Bank of Australia documents released to Bloomberg.

A paper from the RBA's domestic markets division, dated 1 September, estimated that around 5.5% of household financial wealth is held in AI stocks. Most of that exposure comes indirectly through superannuation funds rather than shares held directly, and almost 90% of it is in overseas companies. Drawing on earlier research into how share market wealth affects spending, the paper found that a permanent 20% fall in AI stock prices would leave consumption about 0.7% lower in the long run, rising to around 2.5% if losses spread to the wider equity market. Staff cautioned that the figures may overstate the effect, because households tend to watch their super balances less closely than shares they own directly.

The warning comes as Australians already face a large hit to wealth from falling house prices. A separate RBA paper found that each 1% rise in housing wealth lifts long-run household spending by about 0.16%, with roughly half the effect arriving within two quarters. Bloomberg Economics estimates around A$510 billion of housing wealth has been lost since the end of March. It expects further price falls after the RBA's latest hike to create a drag on spending of A$40 billion to A$50 billion into early 2027.

The documents also show how the RBA judges the labour market. Its models put the NAIRU, the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, at around 5%, but staff apply judgment to lower that assumption to 4.6%, where unemployment stood in August. Staff said they would stay alert to the risk that the true figure is higher. Another document, marked highly restricted, estimated the real neutral interest rate, the inflation-adjusted level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, at between 0.4% and 1.2%.

The papers land at a sensitive point for policy. The RBA raised its cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6% on 29 September, its fourth increase of 2026, as the energy shock from the US-Iran war added to domestic capacity pressures. Headline inflation was 4% in August, well above the 2% to 3% target band. Several economists, including Westpac chief economist and former RBA assistant governor Luci Ellis, expect another hike in November, although household spending was flat in August and the housing market has weakened sharply.

The next main signals for policy will come from the minutes of the September meeting on 13 October and the September-quarter inflation figures on 28 October.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Bullock.

titre: BOJ may signal that inflation has hit 2% target, keeping December rate hike firmly in play
titre_fr: BOJ may signal that inflation has hit 2% target, keeping December rate hike firmly in play
contenu:
Even if there likely won't be another rate hike this month, the BOJ appears to be preparing to take another step towards further policy tightening.

The latest report from Reuters notes that the BOJ could signal in its October quarterly outlook that underlying inflation has roughly reached its 2% target, according to sources familiar with the central bank's thinking.

Now, that's quite significant from a symbolic sense. For a central bank that has spent years trying to generate sustainable inflation, that would mark a meaningful shift in the policy backdrop. And that underscores the readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months.

In other words, the shift is not a guarantee that rate hikes will follow but it does reinforce market expectations of a move in December and perhaps is a suggestion that the BOJ could even step up the pace of its policy tightening.

The sources also point to steady wage gains alongside firmer consumer and wholesale inflation as reasons for the change in tone. They make mention that the recent Tokyo inflation data and the BOJ's Tankan survey have added to confidence that underlying inflation is now close to 2%.

That being said, the report suggests that there is little urgency to move again straight away after having raised interest rates in September already. The sources note that "many" in the central bank would prefer to take a more cautious step in October, wanting to gauge more data on how previous rate hikes are filtering through to the economy.

And markets appear to be thinking along the same lines. Traders are pricing around an 86% chance that the BOJ leaves rates unchanged in October, which looks reasonable after the central bank already moved in September.

The bigger question now is what happens after that.

Markets are currently assigning roughly a 64% chance of another rate hike by December, and any formal acknowledgement that underlying inflation has effectively reached the 2% target would help support that view.

And I would say more importantly, it would fit comfortably with the gradual pace of tightening seen so far. The BOJ has already raised rates in June and again in September, suggesting that policymakers are still trying to normalise policy without moving too aggressively - yet.

I would view this report as being one that treats the October meeting as another piece of groundwork for further tightening.

So if the BOJ is now more comfortable in saying that underlying inflation is around 2%, the debate will then slowly shift towards how quickly rates should rise from here rather than whether further normalisation is justified at all.
